# Book brief (/docs/book-brief)



## What this book is [#what-this-book-is]

This is a practical book you come back to as your life changes. Start with the situation you're in. Work through the steps that fit. Come back when you need the next part.

The book helps readers define the life they want, work out what it costs, and decide what to do from where they are now. It uses facts, stories, worked examples, and exercises they can complete with their own numbers.

There are two parts: the book and an optional [companion workbook](/docs/workbook). The book explains the steps and shows examples. The workbook holds the fill-in pages. Each exercise names its workbook page and gives instructions for doing the same work on plain paper. The book must work on its own.

## The promise [#the-promise]

Your original sentence is still open:

> It's a workbook that gives you a practical step-by-step guide on how to \_\_\_\_\_.

Working direction from [Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2) and [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3): help people make sound money decisions at their current stage and work toward the life they want.

The final promise and book title are still to be chosen.

## Who it's for [#who-its-for]

People have different incomes, debts, priorities, and ideas of a good life. The book meets them at that starting point. It does not assume everyone wants to own a business, work for someone else, or become a millionaire.

The [reader paths](/docs/reader-paths) follow the four situations from Note 3: income with debt, income without debt, no income with debt, and no income without debt. Current income includes support. The four source labels are Employer, Own work, Assets, and Support / retirement. A reader can use more than one.

For someone with no income, the author's first priority is to get income. The larger aim is the life the reader wants. Growing income and reducing debt support that aim. Debt means money owed, including amounts someone calls good debt. Repayment decisions need more detail than that definition alone.

## The shape of the book [#the-shape-of-the-book]

The [chapter plan](/docs/chapters) has 12 chapters. Chapter 1 puts the reader's current money, income, and debt on paper and identifies their path. Seeing the numbers gives the reader a starting point for a plan. Chapter 2 puts a cost on their desired life. Later chapters cover income, paydays, debt, credit, purchases, change, quick-wealth promises, and investing.

Smaller questions belong as sections inside these chapters. Existing topic pages remain writing notes that feed the chapters.

## What each section must give the reader [#what-each-section-must-give-the-reader]

* A clear question and a plain explanation.
* A story or example when it helps explain the point.
* Steps the reader can take, including notes for the relevant reader groups.
* An exercise or decision they can finish, with a companion-workbook page and a plain-paper option.
* Sources for factual claims, figures, rules, and comparisons.
* A next page to use when their situation changes.

## The author's point of view [#the-authors-point-of-view]

The author speaks from experience while still working through his own finances. He is candid about debt, grounded in faith, and interested in helping people make progress without shaming them for their priorities.

Use [Notes 1–9](/docs/raw-thoughts) and the [writing guide](/docs/writing-style) as the voice reference. Preserve the author's questions, everyday examples, directness, and admissions when turning speech into book prose.

## Decisions still open [#decisions-still-open]

The final promise, title, and reader-group symbols remain open. Worked examples use generic $ amounts. Country-specific facts need their own context when drafted. Broad claims in the plan need research before they become finished advice.

Sources: [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan) and [Plan decisions](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions).


# Before we start (/docs/chapters/before-we-start)



## Where I'm coming from [#where-im-coming-from]

Before we go any further, I want you to understand where I'm coming from. As I'm writing this book, I have credit card debt and student loans. I'm blessed to have a job as a software engineer at a fintech company where I earn a good income, and I'm still trying to figure parts of this out myself. Earning money hasn't meant I've made every financial decision well.

I've worked on financial apps, I've invested, and finance is something I spend a lot of time thinking about. There are things I've learned that I think could help someone else. But I'm not coming to you as someone who's done everything perfectly and now has it all sorted out. You'll hear about some of my mistakes as we go.

God told me to write this book, and that's why I'm writing it. Even if what I've learned helps only one person, that's enough for me.

## Your goals are yours [#your-goals-are-yours]

If you picked this up hoping I'd tell you how to become a millionaire, I'm going to disappoint you. Maybe one day, when I'm a millionaire myself, I'll have that book to write. Right now, I want to help you understand your money and make decisions that fit the life you want.

And we don't all want the same life. Some people want to feel secure when they look at their bank account. Some want to travel, some love cars or watches, and some want to know they can cover medical bills for their family. You shouldn't have to feel ashamed because the thing that matters to you is different from what matters to somebody else.

We also have ups and downs. You can earn a good income and still struggle to make it to the next payday, or find yourself dealing with a situation you weren't in a year ago. I want this to be a book you can use where you are now and come back to when that changes. We'll work through what you have, what you owe, and what you want your money to do, so you can see the decisions in front of you.

Continue with [How to use this book](/docs/chapters/how-to-use-this-book).

Draft based on [Note 1](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-1) and [Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2).


# 8. Before you buy (/docs/chapters/before-you-buy)



**First draft · Chapter 8.**

Okay, so you've seen something you want to buy. Maybe it's a new pair of headphones, a camera, or a car you've wanted for a while. You like it, you can already picture yourself using it, and now you're trying to figure out whether you can afford it. What happens to the rest of your money if you go ahead?

I love cars. They make me happy, and I'm not going to pretend that every purchase has to earn me money before it's allowed to matter. Your quality of life matters too. But there's a point where getting the thing you want makes the rest of your life harder, and I don't want you to buy something you can't enjoy because you're worried about the payments.

That's what I want us to work through before you buy it.

## What would it add to your life? [#what-would-it-add-to-your-life]

Start with why you want it. If the answer is that you'd enjoy it, say that. You don't have to turn every want into a business expense to make it sound serious. What matters is being clear about what this purchase adds to your life, so you can decide what you're willing to spend on it.

Then think about what happens if you wait. If waiting means you lose your way to get to work, that needs a different response from continuing to use headphones that still work. A broken fridge and a nicer camera don't need the same answer, even if they cost the same amount.

If the purchase can wait, you've got room to compare a cheaper option, keep using what you have, or save for the one you want. An urgent need asks a different question: how can you meet it with the money and help available to you now? Keep that distinction in mind when we get to my purchase rule. I use it to pause before unplanned spending, not to leave an essential need unmet.

## My “afford it twice” rule [#my-afford-it-twice-rule]

For an unplanned purchase over $250, I try to have enough to pay for it twice. Say I see some new headphones and think, those are sick, I really want them. If they cost $350, I want at least $700 available before I buy them. If I don't have that, I try to leave them alone.

I don't get this right every single time. Something goes on sale and suddenly I've got an explanation for why I should buy it now. That's part of why I use the rule: it gives me something to check when I'm already excited about the purchase. It's a personal rule you can consider, with a threshold that fits your circumstances.

This is for something I haven't been saving for. If you've spent months putting money aside for a purchase, you've already made a plan for it. We still need to check that plan and what you'll have left, but I'm not asking you to save for the same thing twice before using the money you set aside.

Before using the rule, look at which money is actually free for the purchase. If your account has $700 but you need that $700 for rent, you don't have $700 for headphones. Bring forward the bills, debt payments, tax still to cover, saving, giving, and other commitments from [Chapter 4](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid), counting each amount once. Then look at what's left.

Even if you pass that check, you still need to decide whether this is how you want to use the money. Having twice the price available doesn't tell us everything about your circumstances or the other things you care about.

## Let's check the headphones [#lets-check-the-headphones]

Let's try a fictional example in generic dollars, with all purchase charges included and no extra running costs. These are example prices.

| Money today                                                                   |  Amount |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------: |
| Cash already available                                                        |  $1,800 |
| Reserved for bills, debt payments, tax, saving, giving, and other commitments | −$1,100 |
| Free for this decision                                                        |    $700 |

You have $700 free, so the $350 headphones meet my twice-the-price check: $350 × 2 = $700. Now look at what happens to that money under each choice. Passing the check doesn't mean you have to buy them.

| Choice                       | Pay now | Free money left after buying |
| ---------------------------- | ------: | ---------------------------: |
| Buy the $350 headphones      |    $350 |                         $350 |
| Buy a suitable $250 option   |    $250 |                         $450 |
| Keep the headphones you have |      $0 |                         $700 |

Buying the $350 pair leaves $1,450 in the account, which can still look like quite a bit of money. But $1,100 of it belongs to the commitments you already listed, so only $350 remains free. Keep that distinction visible after you buy the headphones; otherwise, you could look at the balance again and spend money you still need for a bill.

Now suppose you have only $350 free because you've been saving that amount for these headphones over time. Since this was a planned purchase, we're checking the plan you made. Has the price changed, or has something happened in your life that means you need the money elsewhere? If your other commitments are still protected and you still want to use the saved $350 this way, you can weigh that choice. Just recognize that buying them would leave no unassigned money in this example. Saving first doesn't remove the need to look at what comes afterward.

You might decide the cheaper pair does everything you need, or that you'd rather keep what you have for now. You could also decide the more expensive pair is worth the difference. Write down your reason and the amount you'd have left, so you're deciding with the whole picture in front of you.

## Money coming in isn't money in your account [#money-coming-in-isnt-money-in-your-account]

I've fallen into this doing software work on the side, and I've done it more than once. You have a conversation with someone about a job, they tell you what they'll pay, and in your head that money is already yours. You're thinking about what you can buy before the payment has even arrived.

For an illustration, say you're expecting $10,000 from a job and you spend $2,000 on a computer because you've counted on that payment. Then life happens: the money doesn't arrive when you expected, but you've already bought the computer. You're left dealing with an expense you took on because of money you thought you were going to have.

If the purchase can wait, wait for the money to arrive. I know how easy it is to tell yourself it's fine because you're getting paid next week. I've made that argument to myself too, and it's a very easy way to get into trouble. When the payment does arrive, check the business costs, tax, and commitments it still has to cover before deciding what you can spend. This applies to next week's wages as well as a freelance job.

The same question comes up with a credit limit. Even if your card has room for a $1,500 camera within its $2,000 limit, we still need to know how you'll pay for the purchase from your own money. Bring it back to the payment plan, and use [Chapter 6](/docs/chapters/credit-cards) to follow what happens on the card bill.

An emergency may leave you with harder choices. Put those choices on paper using Chapter 4's shortfall steps. Don't call an optional purchase an emergency just because you want it today.

## Buy now, pay later still goes in the plan [#buy-now-pay-later-still-goes-in-the-plan]

With buy now, pay later, or BNPL, you get the purchase and spread what you owe across repayments. You're still borrowing the money, even though you're seeing smaller payments at checkout. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes it as a type of instalment loan. The agreement in front of you tells you how that particular plan works, so check it before accepting. [CFPB explanation of BNPL](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-buy-now-pay-later-bnpl-loan-en-2119/).

What worries me is how easy it is to look at one small payment and think, I can manage that. Then you do it with another purchase, and another. They stack up. Each one might look fine when you're looking at it by itself, but you'll have to make those payments from the same money that already covers the rest of your life.

Before you accept, put the full repayment schedule beside the payments you already have. Write what is due today, each later amount and date, any interest or fees, and the total you've agreed to repay. Then check how the provider takes those payments and what happens if you return the item, need a refund, or miss a payment. An agreement you've used before doesn't tell you the terms of the next one.

For example, the CFPB's US guidance notes that a late payment can come with a fee. If an automatic repayment is taken when there isn't enough money in your account, you can also face bank fees. Whether those charges apply depends on the loan and account terms, so include that check when you read them. Other countries have their own rules. [CFPB explanation of BNPL fees](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/do-buy-now-pay-later-bnpl-loans-have-fees-en-2118/).

Let's see how those payments sit beside other purchases. For this invented maths example, the $350 headphones have no interest or fees and are paid for in four payments of $87.50, two weeks apart, starting at checkout. These are assumptions for the calculation, not an offer from a provider.

| Date in the example | New purchase payment | Existing instalment payments | Total due that day |
| ------------------- | -------------------: | ---------------------------: | -----------------: |
| October 10          |               $87.50 |                           $0 |             $87.50 |
| October 12          |                   $0 |                          $60 |                $60 |
| October 19          |                   $0 |                          $90 |                $90 |
| October 24          |               $87.50 |                           $0 |             $87.50 |
| November 7          |               $87.50 |                           $0 |             $87.50 |
| November 21         |               $87.50 |                           $0 |             $87.50 |

Look at the dates before October 24. The first headphone payment is $87.50, but you also have $60 and $90 due on other plans. Together, those three payments need $237.50, on top of your other bills. After that first payment, you still owe $262.50 for the headphones. The other plans may continue beyond the dates we've shown too; the table only includes the dates assumed for this example.

Your debt record and cash calendar show different parts of this same purchase. On the debt record, start with the full $350 obligation and reduce it as you pay. On the calendar, show each actual payment on its date so you know when the cash leaves. Adding $350 and all four payments of $87.50 together would make it look like $700 of spending, when you've only bought one pair of headphones.

If you're already behind on your credit card payments and you're considering another loan for something optional, let's be serious about what you're doing. You already have payments you can't cover. Adding another one gives you more to deal with, even if the amount looks small. Go back to the shortfall or debt plan first.

If you can comfortably keep up with the payments, you can consider the option after comparing the total cost and reading the terms. The important part is looking at all your commitments together, instead of deciding from the size of this one instalment.

## What about a car you really want? [#what-about-a-car-you-really-want]

I love cars. I'm not going to pretend I don't care which one I drive. If a nicer car adds something to your life, you can say that.

For me, I'd want room for twice the payment while still being able to save after mandatory expenses. That's the breathing room I'm thinking about when I say I want to be able to afford the car. But even that personal check needs the rest of the costs beside it. Doubling a payment or choosing a saving percentage won't, on its own, tell you whether a particular car fits your life.

Start with the loan if you're financing the car: how much are you borrowing, what is the annual percentage rate, or APR, and how long will you be making payments? Put the payments and total repayment beside those figures. A monthly payment can look manageable while a longer loan means paying more interest overall, which the CFPB's US guidance explains.

Then add what you'll spend to keep the car: insurance, fuel or charging, maintenance, repairs, registration, and any other ownership costs that apply. Those costs still need money after you've made the loan payment. Use actual local quotes and the contract you're considering so you're comparing the options available to you. [CFPB guide to comparing auto loans](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-compare-auto-loan-offers-what-should-i-look-at-besides-the-monthly-payment-en-753/).

Use the same period when you compare the options, and count the deposit and loan payments once. The payments already cover the financed purchase, so don't add its purchase price again on top of them. Keep annual bills and one-time charges labeled as such. You can set aside money each month for an annual bill, but you still need enough ready by the date the bill is due.

Then ask: what happens in a lower-income month, or when a repair comes up? What would you have to stop paying for? Would this car still improve your life if the payments took away something else you care about?

If it fits and it's something you care about, enjoy it. But if the numbers don't work, you have to be serious with yourself before you sign up. I love cars, and even then, I don't see the point of getting the car I want if I can't enjoy driving it because the payments are making everything else difficult.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Pick one purchase you're considering and work through it on workbook page **[18. My purchase check](/docs/workbook/my-purchase-check)**. You can use plain paper with the same headings. The aim is to leave knowing what you've decided and why, including what you still need to check.

1. **The purchase and the reason.** Write what you want, what it would add to your life, and whether you've planned for it or only just started thinking about it. Then describe what would happen if you waited. That will help you separate something you want today from a need you have to deal with now.
2. **Money available today.** Start with cash you can use, then subtract money already assigned to other commitments once. Keep expected payments separate until they arrive. If you've saved specifically for this purchase, include that fund in the available total; don't subtract it with savings for other purposes or add it a second time. You want to see the money this decision can use.
3. **The choices and full cost.** Put buying this option beside a suitable alternative and, where possible, waiting. For each, include purchase charges, financing costs, and the costs of using it over the same period. Mark any estimates and details you still need to check, so the comparison doesn't look settled before it is.
4. **The payment dates.** Place the upfront amount and every new instalment beside your existing commitments. Keep the full obligation on a separate line, as we did with the headphones. If a later payment depends on income that hasn't arrived, write down that risk and what you'd do if the income were late.
5. **The decision.** Now choose: buy, save first, choose another option, wait, or get more information. Write your reason, what money would remain after the purchase, and your next action or review date. If you've used my twice-the-price rule, label it as a personal check for an unplanned purchase. You still need the rest of the picture you've just worked through.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

| Your path                  | One next chapter                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

# Chapter template (/docs/chapters/chapter-template)



## The reader's question [#the-readers-question]

State the decision this section helps the reader make.

## The explanation [#the-explanation]

Give the reader the concept in plain words. Define any financial term on first use. Follow the [writing guide](/docs/writing-style).

## A story or worked example [#a-story-or-worked-example]

Use an experience from a source note or a clearly labelled example. Keep assumptions, amounts, and currencies visible. Do not invent an event from the author's life.

## What to do [#what-to-do]

Write the steps in order. Make each one specific enough to carry out.

## Notes for each reader group [#notes-for-each-reader-group]

Use the [reader IDs](/docs/reader-paths) for steps that change with income type or debt. Shared guidance applies to all readers.

## Your exercise [#your-exercise]

Give the reader a task with a clear result: a number, a list, a plan, or a decision.

Keep the explanation and worked example in the book. Put blank tables and answer spaces on a named, numbered page in the companion workbook. Link to that page from the exercise. Give the same prompts in plain words so a reader without the workbook can complete every step on paper. Keep unknown details optional where the chapter has not explained them yet.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

Give each relevant reader path one next chapter. Keep the next step clear.

## Source notes and facts to check [#source-notes-and-facts-to-check]

Link to the original Raw thoughts page. Add primary sources for factual claims and record unresolved questions in [Research notes](/docs/research).


# 6. Credit cards 101 (/docs/chapters/credit-cards)



**First draft · All readers.** Use your own card terms beside this chapter. The official guidance linked here is for the United States. Dollar examples are invented teaching examples, not current offers.

## It still has to be paid back [#it-still-has-to-be-paid-back]

Have you ever paid for something with your phone and barely thought about the money? You just tap your phone and keep going, and when you're using a credit card that way, it's easy to forget that you're borrowing money each time. Then the bill comes.

That's what worries me about credit cards. I call them a double-edged sword because there are useful benefits, but the ease of spending can make it feel like you've been given free money. And I'm including myself here. Debt management is something I'm still working on too, so when I say you have to be careful, I'm talking about something I need to pay attention to as well.

So before we talk about points or upgrades, let's look at what you've spent and what it will cost to pay it back. Once you understand the bill, you can decide how the card fits your money plan.

## Which money are you spending? [#which-money-are-you-spending]

A debit card normally uses money in your bank account, while a credit card lets you borrow. They may feel much the same when you tap to pay, but the money comes from different places. Check which account the card uses and whether overdraft is switched on, because overdraft can let a debit payment use money beyond what's in the account too. [CFPB: debit, prepaid, and credit cards](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-are-prepaid-cards-debit-cards-and-credit-cards-different-en-433/).

With a revolving credit card, the agreement allows you to carry an unpaid balance. The lender gives you a **credit limit**, which tells you how much borrowing it allows. So if the limit is $5,000, that's the borrowing limit on the card. You haven't suddenly made another $5,000 that you can add to your income. [Consumer.gov: getting a credit card](https://consumer.gov/credit/getting-credit-card).

A **charge card** starts from a different idea: the bill is due in full each month, although some products add options to carry certain charges. American Express's US terms, for example, separate the amounts you must pay in full from eligible Pay Over Time amounts. Its “no preset spending limit” feature means spending power can change; it doesn't give you unlimited money. Before choosing one, check the terms for that exact product and country, including when payment is due. [American Express US payment terms](https://online.americanexpress.com/myca/shared/summary/paymentcenter/pdf/terms_DDCH.pdf), [Pay Over Time](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/benefits/payment-flexibility/pay-over-time/).

My concern with a card like that is whether you can keep up with what you have to repay. If a pay-in-full bill would be hard for you to manage, take that seriously before applying. Loans, lines of credit, and overdrafts have their own terms too; [Chapter 5](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt) compares those forms of borrowing.

## Three numbers on the bill [#three-numbers-on-the-bill]

When you open the bill, you may see several amounts and wonder which one you're supposed to pay. Start by finding these three labels so you know what each amount is telling you:

| Label               | What you're looking at                                                                      |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Statement balance   | The amount owed when that billing period closed.                                            |
| Current balance     | The posted balance now, including later activity. Pending charges may be separate.          |
| Minimum payment due | The least required for that bill by its due date. It is not the price of clearing the debt. |

You'll also see a **closing date**, when the bill was calculated, and a **payment due date**, which tells you when payment is required. Keep those dates separate as you read the amounts. Your account can still show a statement balance after you've paid it, so check whether the payment has posted and how much is still due. [Capital One: statement and current balances](https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/statement-balance-vs-current-balance/).

Okay, let's walk through an invented card bill with ordinary purchases only. The person using it began with no carried balance and still qualifies for the purchase grace period, which we'll explain below. To keep the example focused, there are no fees, cash advances, special payment plans, refunds, or earlier payments.

| Item                                | Example  |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- |
| Statement closes                    | April 30 |
| Statement balance                   | $800     |
| Minimum due                         | $30      |
| Payment due                         | May 25   |
| New purchase posted on May 3        | $100     |
| Current balance after that purchase | $900     |

The $100 purchase happened after April's bill closed, so it belongs to the next billing period. Under these assumptions, paying $800 by May 25 clears the April statement; paying $900 covers that later purchase too. If you pay only the $30 minimum, you still have $870 of the posted balance unpaid before any later interest or activity, and $770 of that is left from the April statement.

You can see why those labels matter now. If you focus on the $30 in the payment box, it's easy to lose sight of the $900 you owe. Making the required payment and clearing what you've spent are different things.

## When interest starts [#when-interest-starts]

So what happens to the money you haven't paid back? The card's interest terms tell you what borrowing can cost. **APR** means annual percentage rate, but don't read “annual” as meaning you have a year before the lender charges you. Many US issuers calculate interest using daily balances, and different transactions can have different rates. [CFPB: how card interest is calculated](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-does-my-credit-card-company-calculate-the-amount-of-interest-i-owe-en-51/).

Some cards have a **grace period**, which can let you avoid interest on purchases if you meet the pay-in-full terms. It isn't on every card, and if you carry a balance and lose that grace period, new purchases may start earning interest right away. Cash advances generally start accruing interest from the transaction date. That's why we need the terms of your card: read the agreement or ask the issuer what amount you must pay and whether your grace period is active. [CFPB: credit card grace periods](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/).

For a separate, simplified example, let's say $1,000 is subject to interest for all 30 days at a fixed 24% APR. We'll use a 365-day divisor and assume there are no transactions, fees, or daily compounding, with interest added at the end. Under those conditions, the interest works out to:

**$1,000 × 0.24 ÷ 365 × 30 = about $19.73.**

If you then make a $30 payment, the balance becomes about **$989.73**. You sent out $30, but only $10.27 reduced the original $1,000 because the rest covered interest. This is just one period using the assumptions above, so it doesn't give us a payoff date or reproduce every issuer's method. It does let us see where that payment went.

That's why making the minimum payment on time and avoiding borrowing costs are separate questions. You can satisfy that month's required payment while still paying to carry the rest. If you have money to pay more after covering your other needs, use the debt plan in [Chapter 5](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt) to decide where that extra money goes. [Consumer.gov: minimum payments](https://consumer.gov/credit/getting-credit-card).

Interest isn't the only cost to check. An annual fee can still apply in a year when you avoid purchase interest, and cash advances, transfers, late payments, or foreign purchases may have separate charges. Copy the amounts and conditions from your agreement so you can see the costs together. If you're using a promotional rate, include when it ends and what terms follow it. [CFPB: credit card terms](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/credit-cards/answers/key-terms/).

## What did the reward cost you? [#what-did-the-reward-cost-you]

I like the idea of getting something back from spending I was already going to do. But that last part matters. Was I already going to do it?

I got an Amex Gold card with an offer that required me to spend a certain amount to get the bonus. If you have costs you were already going to pay and can put those on the card, that's one thing. But you have to be careful about what happens next. You start moving purchases onto it, then buying extra things to reach the target, and you're spending, spending, spending. Before you know it, you owe a lot of money. The bonus is still tied to money you have to repay.

Suppose a fictional card offers a 2% cash reward. The $500 purchase you already planned earns $10 if it qualifies. But if you add $100 of things you didn't want just to earn points, that extra spending earns $2. You've now spent $100 to get $2 back, leaving $98 less in your money plan. That's the part you have to account for when the reward is tempting you to spend more.

Or suppose you pay a $100 annual fee and redeem $80 of rewards over the year. Before considering any other costs or benefits, you're $20 behind. To decide what the card gives you overall, add up the benefits you use and subtract the fees and interest you pay. Be realistic about what those benefits are worth to you: a hotel credit shouldn't get full value in your calculation if you'd never book that hotel without it.

These are invented examples, and real rewards have their own rules for eligible spending, deadlines, fees, and redemption. Check those before taking an offer, then come back to the spending itself. Can you pay for it without relying on money that hasn't arrived?

## Make the payment a real plan [#make-the-payment-a-real-plan]

Now take the money available after essential needs and your other commitments, and use that to choose a payment amount. Write down when you'll pay and which account the money will come from, allowing for the issuer's processing time and cutoff. You don't want the due date to be the first time you try to work all of that out.

Automatic payment can help you follow through, but check whether you've selected the minimum, the statement balance, or a fixed amount. Those settings can send very different amounts out of your account. You still need enough money in the linked account and a check that the payment went through, so keep a reminder even if you've turned automatic payment on. [FTC: using credit cards and paying bills](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/using-credit-cards-and-disputing-charges).

If you can't make the minimum, contact the issuer promptly, explain what you can afford, and ask what help is available. If they propose an arrangement, you need to understand what happens to interest, fees, future payments, card use, and reporting. Get the terms in writing before relying on them, because making the call by itself doesn't mean a change has been approved. [CFPB: act fast if you can't pay](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_adult-fin-ed_act-fast-pay-credit-cards.pdf).

And if the choice is a card payment or food, don't hide that problem under a rewards calculation. Use the shortfall work in [Chapter 4](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid) and the debt review in Chapter 5. We need to plan for the situation you're in.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Have your statement beside you for this part. Workbook **[page 15: My card statement](/docs/workbook/my-card-statement)** helps you understand the bill, and **[page 16: My card payment plan](/docs/workbook/my-card-payment-plan)** takes you through deciding what to pay. If you're using plain paper, use one sheet per card with the same headings. And if you don't have a card, practice with the $800 statement above; there's no reason to apply for anything to complete this exercise.

1. **Read the record.** Give the card a nickname and write its issuer and country, leaving full account numbers off the worksheet. Then bring over the statement date, current-balance date, balances, pending activity, minimum, and due date. Keeping those dates beside the amounts will help you tell what the bill covers and what has happened since.
2. **Find the cost.** Look through the terms for the purchase rate, any other rates that apply, fees, and any promotion end date, and copy them onto the page. Find out whether you have a purchase grace period and what preserves or restores it, then write that down too. For anything unclear, leave yourself the note “ask issuer.” You'll know what still needs an answer before you rely on it.
3. **Choose a funded payment.** Work out what's available for this card after your other commitments, then record that amount alongside the payment you choose, the bank account it will come from, and the date. Check your payday plan as you do this: if it already includes the payment, don't add it again.
4. **See what remains.** Estimate what you'll owe after the payment, marking any interest you don't yet know and any pending charges. Use that picture to decide how you'll handle new spending. If you can't meet the required amount, your next step is the contact action discussed above; write what you'll do and when.
5. **Check the result.** When the payment should have posted, check whether it did and record the result. Update your debt record with the amount now owed and set the next review date, so the plan follows what happened in the account.

For the fictional $800 statement, a completed plan might say: “I have $900 reserved for this card. I'll pay the $800 statement before May 25, using the issuer's confirmed timing. I'll keep $100 reserved for the May 3 purchase. I'll check that the payment posted.” Notice where the remaining $100 is going: it's already committed to the later purchase, so you can't treat it as spare spending money.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

| Your path                     | Next chapter                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| I-D · Income with debt        | [7. Credit scores 101](/docs/chapters/credit-scores), after setting this payment and any needed help in motion.          |

# 7. Credit scores 101 (/docs/chapters/credit-scores)



**First draft · All readers.** This chapter uses the United States as its worked system. Reports, scores, access, and rules differ by country. The exercise starts by finding the system that applies to you.

## What does that number actually tell you? [#what-does-that-number-actually-tell-you]

Okay, so what is a credit score, and why does this number matter when you want to borrow money?

If you're about to borrow for a home, you want to understand what the lender is looking at. At the same time, if you can't pay for food this week, checking the number over and over won't put money in your account. We need to understand what a score can tell us so we know when to use it and what else still needs our attention.

In the US system, the score helps estimate credit behavior, such as whether someone will repay a loan on time. To produce that number, a company takes information from a credit report and applies a formula called a **scoring model**. A lender may then use the result to help decide whether to lend to you and what terms to offer. [CFPB: what a credit score is](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-score-en-315/).

A score doesn't tell me the life you want, the people you care for, or what you've had to deal with. Those are the things we started with, and they still matter as we work through the credit side. The score gives us one piece of information we may need along the way.

## The report and the score [#the-report-and-the-score]

First, let's separate the report from the score, because they're easy to mix up. A **credit report** is a record that can contain your accounts, balances, payment history, and requests to check your credit. Credit reporting companies collect that information from lenders and other sources. In the US, the three nationwide bureaus are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and their records can differ because a lender doesn't have to report to all three. [CFPB: credit reports](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-report-en-309/), [Consumer.gov: checking your report](https://consumer.gov/credit/checking-your-credit-report).

A **score** is calculated using that kind of information. FICO, for example, is a scoring provider; it isn't another name for Equifax. So when you're looking at a number, there are two things to find out: which report supplied the information and which scoring model used it.

That helps explain why you might see different scores in different places. The model, the source of its information, and the date can all change the result. Even the score in your banking app may differ from the one a lender uses for a particular product, so there isn't one number that every lender sees. [CFPB: why scores vary](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-score-en-315/).

So when someone says, “My score is good,” we need a little more detail. Which score are they looking at, and when was it calculated? What are they hoping to be approved for? Seeing 720 or 750 doesn't mean every lender will approve the application.

### Where did scores come from? [#where-did-scores-come-from]

One part of the history is the introduction of the US FICO Score, which FICO dates to 1989. Credit reporting existed before then, so that date tells us when this particular scoring system arrived. It doesn't tell us when every country began judging credit. [FICO's history of its score](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/blog/history-of-the-fico-score).

The useful thing to understand is why a system like this exists: it helps people make lending decisions. You can learn how it works and use that knowledge when you need it, while still working toward the life you chose in Chapter 2.

## When it can matter [#when-it-can-matter]

Borrowing is one reason to pay attention to this information, because it can affect both the application and the price of a loan. But in the US, reports can also be used in some housing, insurance, service, and employment decisions. What someone is allowed to use and whether they need consent vary, so ask what they'll check for the decision you're making. They may check a report without using a credit score. [CFPB: uses of credit reports](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-report-en-309/).

Before you apply, ask what the process involves and what you can review first. Then bring the decision back to your own money. If the offer is approved, can you make the payments and still cover the other things you need? You still have to do that calculation even when the lender says yes.

Let's say a lender offers a fictional reader a $450 monthly payment, but after essentials and existing commitments, that person has $200 left each month. They're $250 short before we even allow for any new costs. Whatever score helped them get the offer, they still need to work out how the payment would fit.

That's why the report and your money plan need to sit beside each other when you're considering an important application.

## What to check behind the number [#what-to-check-behind-the-number]

Payment history, unpaid balances, account history, and new applications can affect scores, though the weight given to each depends on the model. Rather than guessing how many points one move will add, we can start by checking the information behind the number. [CFPB: score factors](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-score-en-315/).

Look through the accounts and see whether you recognize them, whether the balances and payment records look right, and whether closed accounts are marked correctly. If you see an application you don't remember, make a note to check it. Pay attention to the report's dates as you compare it with your statements: a balance from an earlier date may differ from today's balance without being wrong.

One term you'll come across for cards is **utilization**, meaning how much of the available credit is being used. To calculate a simple card percentage, divide the balance by the limit and multiply by 100. FICO says its scores consider revolving-credit use, but remember that the balance reported to a bureau may differ from what you see in the account today. [FICO: amounts owed](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-scores/amount-of-debt).

Let's use an invented example to see how the calculation works for one card and then for two cards together:

| Card     | Reported balance | Reported limit | Balance ÷ limit |
| -------- | ---------------- | -------------- | --------------- |
| A        | $600             | $2,000         | 30%             |
| B        | $0               | $3,000         | 0%              |
| Combined | $600             | $5,000         | 12%             |

For the combined figure, we added the dollar balances and limits before dividing, which gives us 12%. Averaging 30% and 0% would give a different answer because the two limits aren't the same. This illustration uses two ordinary revolving cards with reported limits; other products can be handled differently.

Now, does that calculation tell us whether this person can afford the $600? We still need their money plan for that. It tells us how much of the available credit is being used. Treating 30% as a spending allowance would mean buying something because the card has room, without checking whether you have the money to pay for it.

The CFPB advises paying on time and keeping balances low relative to limits. It also says you don't need to carry a card balance to build a good score, so there's no need to pay interest just because you think keeping a balance will help the number. [CFPB: building credit](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-and-keep-a-good-credit-score-en-318/).

If you're new to credit and can't see a score, check the provider's explanation before assuming something is wrong. A model may not have enough history to produce one yet, which is different from producing a low score. Understanding which situation you're in helps you decide what to do next. [CFPB: understanding credit scores](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_ymyg_want-credit-to-work-for-you_booklet_print.pdf).

## Does checking hurt your score? [#does-checking-hurt-your-score]

The answer depends on what kind of check you're talking about. In US credit reporting, checking your own report is a **soft inquiry**, a category that also includes certain reviews and prescreening checks. Those checks don't affect your credit scores. A **hard inquiry**, which commonly follows a credit application, can affect them. [CFPB: credit inquiries](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-inquiry-en-1317/).

If you see a button that says “see if you qualify,” read what happens when you press it. The process isn't necessarily the same everywhere, so ask which step involves a hard inquiry before agreeing to it.

Checking your own report lets you see what's there before you decide whether to borrow. You can do that without making a loan application.

## Read it, then act on what you find [#read-it-then-act-on-what-you-find]

If you're in the United States, you can start with [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/), where the three nationwide bureaus offer free weekly online reports as checked on October 1, 2026. Keep the report and score distinction in mind here too: access to those reports doesn't promise a free score from every provider. [Consumer.gov: free reports](https://consumer.gov/credit/checking-your-credit-report).

If you live elsewhere, start with your country's official consumer regulator or credit-report access service, then confirm the provider, cost, and terms before sharing personal information. You don't need to buy a monitoring subscription to complete this exercise.

If you find something wrong on a US report, take that specific item to both the bureau showing it and the business that supplied it through their dispute process. Explain what is wrong and what correction you're asking for, with copies of the records that support you. Keep your own copies and the response so you can follow what happens. If you suspect identity theft, use [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov/) as well. [CFPB: disputing an error](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-an-error-on-my-credit-report-en-314/).

Let's say our fictional reader sees a balance on an account they already paid off. They check when the report was updated and compare it with the payoff receipt. If it still appears wrong, they have something specific to ask about or dispute, with records to support it. That gives them an action they can take: send the payoff record about this account and check the response. A goal of raising the score by 50 points wouldn't tell them how to deal with the account in front of them.

If the information is accurate and you don't like what you're seeing, you can still use it to decide what to do next. Bring the payment problem into your debt plan, work out what you can pay, and ask for help if it doesn't fit. We can't promise a particular score or approval date from any one action here, but we can choose a next step based on what's in the report.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

For this exercise, we're going to look at your own records and leave with one next action. Use **[workbook page 17: My credit check](/docs/workbook/my-credit-check)**, or draw five boxes on plain paper: my purpose, my report, any score shown, things to check, and my next action. Keep the report documents somewhere private and use account nicknames on the worksheet; you don't need to copy the full account details into it.

1. **Name the purpose.** Start with why you're checking: you might be looking for errors, preparing for an application, or simply learning what's on file. Write that purpose along with the country and the official source you'll use, so the check fits the decision you need to make.
2. **Record what you got.** Write the bureau, the report date, and the date shown for the item you're reviewing. If there's a score too, record its model, provider, data source, date, and scale where shown. Use “not shown” for anything you can't see. You can still do useful work with the report alone.
3. **Check the records.** Put the report beside your own records and compare the account names, balances, limits, payment history, and any unfamiliar inquiries. If something appears wrong, write down the exact item and the evidence that makes you question it. That will help you explain the possible error when you follow up.
4. **Choose one action.** Based on what you found, decide whether the next step is to check with the provider, submit a supported dispute, or adjust an existing payment plan. Give that action a date and keep the response, so you can see whether it resolved the issue.
5. **Set a review point.** Write what you're waiting for and when you'll follow up. If you're doing this before an application, bring its estimated costs and payments into your money plan too; checking the report is one part of preparing for that decision.

A filled line could read: “Purpose: check records before a future housing application. Item: paid account still shows $400. Evidence: payoff receipt and report update date. Action: ask the provider to check, then use the dispute process if needed. Review: October 15.” The $400 and date are invented; this isn't a forecast of when a correction will happen.

# 3. Find and grow your income (/docs/chapters/grow-your-income)



**First draft · Chapter 3.**

If you have no income coming in, the first thing we need to figure out is how to get some. It's hard to make plans for the future when you have no way to cover what's happening right now. Keep the life you described in Chapter 2, but let's start with what could bring money in from where you are today.

If money already comes in, we have a different question to work through. You might need more money, different hours, or work you enjoy more. Look at the gap you wrote down and the day you want to have. That will help us decide which change to work on, instead of chasing a bigger number without asking what comes with it.

You don't need to settle the rest of your career in this chapter. I want you to leave with one step you can take and a reason for taking it.

## If no money comes in [#if-no-money-comes-in]

I think that if you can work, need income, and have nothing coming in, you need to apply for work you can do. Some people aren't going to like that, especially if they've spent years getting a degree and had a particular company or role in mind. But if you're passing over suitable jobs simply because the company isn't the one you pictured, I'm sorry, that doesn't make sense to me. Apply. Give yourself a chance to earn something while you work towards the next thing.

Now, being a stay-at-home parent is a full-time responsibility. If that's what you want and it works for your household, there's nothing wrong with it. Studying can also take all the time you have. Your health, care duties, transport, or permission to work may limit what's possible too. A job you can't get to or fit around care doesn't become an option just because someone tells you to take it.

I'm talking about the work you can do. Write down the hours you have, where you can get to, and any costs you'd have to cover before the first payment arrives. Then look at the roles and employers that fit those limits. You may need help with an application or support while you search, and those are steps you can take as well.

Even a temporary job can be part of the plan. Taking it doesn't mean you've decided to stay there forever or given up on the life you want. You can earn from something else and keep looking for the role you want, after checking that the hours, costs, and terms of the temporary work make sense for you.

If there's already a gap for food, housing, or other essentials, put that on the page now. A possible job next month won't pay this week's bill, so check the help available where you live while you work on getting income. We need to deal with what's happening now as well as where you're trying to go.

## What are you actually trying to get to? [#what-are-you-actually-trying-to-get-to]

I had a conversation with someone at Starbucks about having a goal and choosing how to get there. Sometimes you get so set on one way of doing something that you don't stop to consider another route. You might not even know another route exists.

Think about trying to reach the top of a sand dune in a Ferrari. You've decided you want the Ferrari, and now you're putting all your effort into getting it up the sand. But what was the goal? If it was getting to the top, why are you so attached to doing it in that car? You could at least consider a Jeep or an ATV before spending all that time trying to make the Ferrari work.

For me, it was being a tech founder. I'd put so much effort into that idea, but when I thought about what mattered to me, it was having a say in how a product works, how it's designed, and how it's built. Being a founder was the way I'd pictured getting that decision-making power. Once I understood what I wanted from it, I could ask whether there were other ways to get there.

So when you look at an income option, ask what you want it to give you. The pay matters, but so might the hours, the chance to make things, or being there when your children get home. If several routes could give you those things, consider them. You don't have to start a business because someone else did, or leave a job that works for your life just to prove you're ambitious.

## If an employer pays you [#if-an-employer-pays-you]

You can start with the job you have as well as looking at other jobs. More hours, a higher rate, or a different role could help, but think about what each would mean for your week. If the extra hours take away something you need at home, include that in the decision.

Before a pay conversation, gather examples of the work you've done and check what comparable roles pay in your area. That gives you something specific to discuss. Compare the whole offer too, including benefits, hours, and travel, so you can see what you'd gain and what you'd have to change. There isn't always room to negotiate, but you can prepare to ask.

Here's a sample way to start:

> I'd like to talk about my pay. Here are the responsibilities I've taken on and the results I can show. What would need to happen for my pay to increase, and when could we review it?

If another role needs a skill you don't yet have, read the job listings before paying for training. See what employers ask for and how much of it you already know. “I need to learn more” can go on forever; finding a specific skill you need lets you decide how to practice it and whether the training you're considering would help.

## If you want to earn from your own work [#if-you-want-to-earn-from-your-own-work]

Okay, so you want to write, edit, build an app, or sell a service. Who would pay you, and what would they get? Work backwards from that. If you're going to spend time making something, you need to figure out whether someone wants it enough to pay for it.

Write an answer a person could understand, then choose a way to test it with time and money you can afford to use. You might speak to possible customers, show them a sample, or offer one small paid job with a clear scope. You can learn from that before committing more of what you have.

As you do it, keep track of the money and the work involved. What customers pay you is revenue, and some of that may have to cover business costs. Tax may still need to come out of what's left. Until you've accounted for those amounts, you don't know how much of the payment you can use for your own plan.

Let's use an invented example with generic dollars. Suppose you complete four editing jobs at $150 each. All four customers pay during the period you're reviewing.

| This batch of work                                         |        Amount |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------: |
| Four paid jobs × $150                                      | $600 received |
| All business costs for this batch, assumed for the example |         −$120 |
| Left before tax                                            |          $480 |
| Time delivering the work                                   |       8 hours |
| Time finding customers and doing admin                     |       4 hours |
| Total time                                                 |      12 hours |

Divide the $480 by all 12 hours and you get $40 before tax for each hour you counted. In this example, that's what remains after the business costs we've listed; it isn't a wage offer or take-home pay. If you discover more costs or hours, change the calculation. And you still need to find the next customer. Four people paying you this time doesn't tell you that four more will come next week.

That's the work I want you to think through: finding a customer, doing what you agreed to do, and checking what's left after the time and costs involved. Keep writing or building if it matters to you, but keep hoped-for earnings separate from money you have today. You can work towards an income goal without treating it as income you've already earned.

## Income can come from more than one place [#income-can-come-from-more-than-one-place]

As you compare options, keep using the four labels from Chapter 1: **Employer, Own work, Assets, and Support / retirement.** Hourly pay and salary both sit under Employer, and you can use several labels if money comes from different places.

If you already receive money from an asset, start with what it paid you and record any costs or tax still to cover. We need that payment to know what it contributes, because owning something doesn't tell us that it pays you each month. Work with the receipts you have here; don't treat this exercise as a reason to buy an investment to fill an immediate gap.

If you receive support or retirement payments, include the amounts you can use and check the provider's terms before assuming a payment will change or continue. If you're looking for US programs, [USAGov's benefit finder](https://www.usa.gov/benefit-finder) links to possible benefits and application information. Elsewhere, check your local official services.

Help with a cost still matters, even when nobody pays cash into your account; just record that noncash help separately from money you can spend. Keep borrowed money and money taken from savings separate from ongoing income too. They change today's balance without creating a new source of earnings.

You can return to [Chapter 1's income map](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) if you're unsure where a payment belongs. These groups help you build the plan, while a tax office may classify the same payment differently.

## When does the money arrive? [#when-does-the-money-arrive]

A monthly total can look fine while one week is difficult because the payment hasn't arrived yet. Write down the date as well as the amount, and mark each payment as received, expected, or uncertain. You may have done the work and sent the invoice, but until it's paid, you still don't have that money available.

If payments vary, look at several periods in your records so you can see the low periods alongside the better ones. Don't build the whole plan around your best month and assume every month will go that way. We'll work through payment dates in Chapter 4; for now, collect them and keep money still to come separate from money you already have.

## Back to Michelle [#back-to-michelle]

Remember Michelle, our fictional reader from [Chapter 2](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want). The household life she priced costs $8,400 a month. Her partner's agreed contribution is $2,400, leaving $6,000 for her to cover. With $3,000 in take-home pay from customer service, she has a gap of $3,000 a month.

But Michelle also hates the work she's doing. She wants to spend her day writing and researching, and she wants to be available for school pickup. She could come home angry, spend the evening scrolling or watching TV, and do the same thing again tomorrow. I don't think that gets her where she wants to go. She needs to give some time to figuring out what else she could do, while remembering that her current job still brings money in.

Let's give her three routes to check against both the income goal and the day she wants. These are possibilities to investigate, not claims about available jobs or market pay.

| Possible route                 | What she needs to find out                                                         | A first step                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| A writing or research job      | Required skills, actual pay, hours, and school-pickup fit                          | Compare three current job listings                    |
| Paid editing alongside her job | Whether someone will pay for a defined piece of work, and what it takes to deliver | Make one sample and speak to three possible customers |
| Her own book or blog           | Who it serves and how it might eventually earn money                               | Test one piece with its intended readers              |

In this example, she decides to explore editing while keeping her current job. She can give it two hours this week without spending any money on the first check. By Friday, she'll make a short sample using text she owns and ask three possible customers about their needs.

Then on Sunday, she can look at what happened. Did anyone have the problem she wants to solve, and was there interest in paying her for a defined job? Would doing that work fit her week? If the answers don't support it, she can change the offer or look more closely at the job route.

She still has the $3,000 gap, and we can't give her the fictional $480 from the editing example just because she's made a plan. What she's done is choose something she can try, with a point at which she'll review it. That gives her information for the next decision before she puts more time or money into it.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Take what you've learned about your options and work through it on workbook page **[8. My income options](/docs/workbook/my-income-options)** and page **[9. My next income step](/docs/workbook/my-next-income-step)**. If you're using plain paper, use those page names and the headings below. We're going to narrow the options to something you can try.

1. **My starting point.** Write your reader path and the sources you already have, then say whether you need money for now or are working towards a change for later. If you've done Chapter 2, bring over your target and gap so you can refer to them as you compare choices. If you haven't, you can still start here with the need you have today.
2. **My limits.** Think through what it would take to fit this step into your life. Write down the hours you have, care needs, travel, work requirements, and how much money you can afford to put into it. If there's no money available, write “none.” That belongs in the plan because it affects which options you can try.
3. **Two options.** For each option, write who would pay you, what you'd do, and the costs and time involved. Beside that, explain what evidence you have and what you still don't know, so you can see what needs checking. Keep expected earnings separate from your current income. If only one option is feasible, record why; you don't need to invent a second one to fill the page.
4. **One action.** Choose something you can do by a date, such as finishing an application, having a pay or customer conversation, or checking with a support provider. Give it a time limit and a spending limit, so you've decided how much you can put into this step before you start.
5. **A review date.** Decide what you'll check and when you'll come back to it. Keep payment dates on a separate part of the page, noting whether each payment has arrived. Before comparing any new amount with a take-home target, check what costs and tax still need to come out. If you've already subtracted a cost to reach that amount, don't take it off again.

Try to leave with a sentence you can act on. If all you've written is “I want more money,” go back and name what you're going to do tomorrow. “I'll finish this application by Thursday” gives you a task you can start and a date to work towards.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

| Your path                  | What to do from here                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| N-D · No income, with debt | Take your income or support step. Use Chapter 4 to plan from money actually available and handle a shortfall; don't wait for a hoped-for payment. |
| N-ND · No income, no debt  | Take your income or support step, then use Chapter 4 to plan available money and the first payment when it comes.                                 |
| I-D · Income, with debt    | Use Chapter 4 to plan existing income, bills, and debt payments while you work on your chosen income step.                                        |
| I-ND · Income, no debt     | Use Chapter 4 to plan existing income around your costs and goals while you test the change you've chosen.                                        |

Each of these paths takes you to **[4. When you get paid](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid)**, where we'll work with the money available to you. Keep the action you've chosen here beside your money picture so you can continue it while you plan what to do with the money coming in.

# How to use this book (/docs/chapters/how-to-use-this-book)



## Start where you are [#start-where-you-are]

You don't have to read this book from front to back before you can do anything with it. Start with the part that fits your life right now, whether you have income and debt, have no income coming in, or are trying to work out what to do with the money you have.

If you're unsure where to begin, [Chapter 1: Start where you are](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) will help you put your situation on paper. From there, it gives you one next chapter to use. That way, you've got somewhere to start without having to work through every topic first.

## Put it to work [#put-it-to-work]

As you go through a section, read the explanation and work through the example before trying it with your own numbers. The example helps you see how the idea works; the exercise is where you find out what it means for your life.

The book explains each step, and the [companion workbook](/docs/workbook) gives you space to write your answers. When I say “go to workbook page 1,” that's where you'll find the matching exercise.

If you don't have the companion workbook, a notebook or plain paper is fine. Each exercise tells you what to write, so you can do every step without buying anything else. You can also use a document you keep beside you if that works better than writing by hand.

You're probably not going to remember every single thing you read in here, and you don't need to. Come back when you get paid, when you're thinking about a purchase, or when your situation changes and you need to work through a different problem. The reader-group labels from Chapter 1 will help you find the steps and notes that fit.

## Work toward your own life [#work-toward-your-own-life]

Keep the life you want in mind as you use the book. You might want to travel more, or you might want a job you enjoy that lets you come home and have dinner with your family every night. Those are different goals, and they'll ask different things of your money.

[Chapter 2: The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want) helps you describe that life and put a cost on it. Then we can work backward to the choices you can make from where you are.

Draft based on [Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2), [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3), the [general plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan), and the [companion-workbook decision](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions#the-book-and-a-companion-workbook).
