# 5. Make a plan for debt (/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt)



**First draft · Chapter 5.**

What do you do when you owe money and the money coming in already has somewhere to go?

I've been there. I lost my job during my honeymoon, and my wife and I moved to New York with debt from our wedding. She was a full-time student, our costs had gone up, and I didn't have a job. I spent a lot of time living on credit because there were still bills to pay. It put me in a hole, and getting out was something I was still trying to figure out.

So I'm not going to talk to you like looking at a balance fixes everything. I know what it's like to owe money while trying to figure out where the next money is going to come from. Writing it down gives us somewhere to start, because we need to know what we're dealing with before we can decide what to do about it.

In Chapter 1, you wrote what you owe. Now we're going to add the details: what it costs, what is due, and what happens if you can't pay. Then we'll choose a next step you can actually take.

## Put every amount on the page [#put-every-amount-on-the-page]

When I say debt, I mean money you owe, including the loan you took out for a useful reason and the money a friend lent you for rent. You may have a good reason for borrowing it, but you still have to account for paying it back. Calling it “good debt” doesn't remove the payment.

Use the same three groups from Chapter 1:

| Group                                   | What to look for                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Borrowing or credit                     | Loans, cards, lines of credit, money borrowed from people, buy now pay later balances |
| Unpaid bills                            | Amounts already owed for rent, utilities, medical care, or other services             |
| Taxes, fines, and court-ordered amounts | Amounts due to a government or under a court order                                    |

Include a bill you already owe even if it isn't late. Next month's planned spending belongs in your payment plan; a purchase you haven't made yet isn't a debt. And if you look at an amount and think, “I don't owe that,” mark it for checking. We need to keep track of the dispute without treating the amount as settled or making it disappear from the page.

Now get the latest statement or agreement for each balance so we can add the details. The person or company you owe is your **creditor**. Write their name, the balance and the date you checked it, then the amount due and its due date. Look for the rate, fees, and anything already overdue. If you can't find something, write “unknown” and make a note to ask. Leaving it unknown is more useful than planning as though the cost is zero.

Canada's financial consumer agency also includes lenders, unpaid service providers, government, and people in its [debt explanation](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/debt/plan-debt-free.html).

## What did you agree to? [#what-did-you-agree-to]

Let's say two people each owe $5,000. One has five years to repay it, while the other has a payment overdue today. We can't give them the same next step just because the balances match. We need to know what each person agreed to and what is happening with that agreement now.

The money borrowed is called the **principal**, and **interest** is a borrowing cost charged using a rate. There may be fees on top of that. This matters when you make a payment: some of it can go toward interest or fees, so the amount you borrowed may fall by less than the amount you paid. Your statement should help you see where the payment went. [FCAC: debt costs.](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/debt/plan-debt-free.html)

You also need to know whether the borrowing puts something you own at risk. With **secured** borrowing, an asset is pledged as backup, called **collateral**, and the lender may be able to take it if the agreement isn't met. **Unsecured** borrowing has no pledged asset, but leaving it unpaid still has consequences. What can happen depends on the contract and local law. [FCAC: personal loans, Canadian guidance.](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/personal-loans.html)

### A loan, a line of credit, or an overdraft? [#a-loan-a-line-of-credit-or-an-overdraft]

You might be offered a loan, a line of credit, or overdraft borrowing. Here's how those common structures generally work, along with what to look for in the actual offer before deciding what it would cost you.

| Product                  | How it generally works                                                            | What to check                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Personal instalment loan | Receive a set amount and repay through scheduled payments.                        | Payment, end date, rate, fees, and early-repayment costs.                 |
| Line of credit           | Borrow up to a limit. Repaying can make room to borrow again under the agreement. | Rate changes, fees, required payments, and how to reduce the balance.     |
| Overdraft borrowing      | The bank covers a payment your account can't cover, leaving money owed to it.     | Interest, fees, repayment deadline, and what happens to the next deposit. |

The comparison uses Canadian official guidance for [personal loans](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/personal-loans.html), [lines of credit](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/loans-lines-credit.html), and [overdraft protection](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/banking/overdraft-protection.html). Terms elsewhere can differ.

A line of credit may have a changing rate, and if its required payment covers only interest, making that payment won't reduce the amount you borrowed. Even if the rate is lower than another product's, it's still borrowed money that needs to be repaid. [FCAC: lines of credit.](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/loans-lines-credit.html)

With overdraft protection, the question is where the money comes from when the payment goes through. A transfer from your own savings uses your money, while a transfer from a credit line adds borrowing. Both may involve fees, so check which one you have and what it costs. [FCAC: overdraft protection.](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/banking/overdraft-protection.html)

Cards get their own explanation in Chapter 6, where we'll look at the bill and what the different payment amounts mean.

### Look past “good” and “bad” [#look-past-good-and-bad]

What did the debt help you do? Maybe it covered an emergency, bought something you still use, or paid for study or work that you hope will help later. Write that down, because the purpose is part of the decision. Then put the payment beside your income and the things you need to pay for now. A useful purpose doesn't guarantee the result you wanted, and even if borrowing made sense at the time, we still need to check whether the payment fits today.

If you're thinking about moving current debt into a new loan, compare the full repayment amount, fees, time, and any asset at risk. The balance is still there after you move it, and a smaller monthly payment can mean paying for longer. You need the total cost as well as the monthly amount before deciding. [FCAC: comparing loan options.](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/personal-loans.html)

## Deal with urgent consequences first [#deal-with-urgent-consequences-first]

Sometimes there isn't enough to pay everything. I'm not going to pretend that never happens, because I've been in that situation too. What I do is look at what absolutely needs to be paid and put those things in order. If rent is later in the month, paying a smaller, less important bill today can still leave you without the rent money when you need it. That's why we need to look at the whole situation before sending money out.

Before deciding which debt to pay down faster, look at what you need for food, medicine, housing, essential utilities, and keeping your income coming in. Put insurance and court-ordered payments in that review too. For each one, the question is what could happen if you miss it and how soon that could happen. If your housing is at risk, that needs attention even when another debt has a higher rate. The CFPB's [bill-priority tool](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_prioritizing-bills_tool.pdf) uses those consequences to help you make the short-term choice.

If there is a gap, use Chapter 4's shortfall plan and contact the creditor or provider through a verified channel to ask what help is available. Before relying on an option, find out what it costs and record what they actually agree to, including dates and interest. Asking for a change doesn't change the agreement by itself. [CFPB: unpaid bills](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_prioritizing-bills_tool.pdf); [FCAC: discussing loan payments](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/personal-loans.html).

If you're on the **N-D** path, finding income or support is still a priority. An urgent notice may need a response before that income arrives, though, so keep working on the income step while you get help with the payment problem in front of you.

## Choose where extra money goes [#choose-where-extra-money-goes]

Once you've covered current needs and required payments, we can look at whether there's money for extra repayment. Remember the costs you know are coming too. If you send away the money you need for food, you'll still have to figure out how to buy food afterward. We want a payment amount you can manage alongside the rest of your life.

There are two common ways to choose where the extra money goes:

* **Highest rate first:** you keep up the required payments on your debts and put the extra toward the one with the highest rate, so you're targeting the interest cost.
* **Smallest balance first:** you keep up the required payments and put the extra toward clearing the smallest balance. Finishing that one may help you keep going, though this approach can cost more interest.

You may hear these called the avalanche and snowball methods; the CFPB [compares both](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-reduce-your-debt/). We're choosing between them after dealing with urgent consequences, and we still need to check for special terms that could affect the decision, such as a promotional rate about to end or a fee for paying early.

Choose a method you understand and write down why it fits your situation. That gives you something to come back to when your income, costs, or debt terms change. The name is less useful than understanding where the money is going and why you've chosen to send it there.

### Sam's first month [#sams-first-month]

Let's work through a month with Sam, a fictional reader. The generic dollar amounts and contract terms below are invented to show the steps, not taken from a lender's offer.

Sam has $3,000 take-home income this month. His payday plan reserves $2,400 for all non-debt needs and planned costs, plus $100 for unexpected needs. There are no overdue bills, collection notices, or urgent legal payments in this example. That leaves **$500 for all debt payments**.

| Debt                 | Opening balance |      Annual rate | Required payment this month |
| -------------------- | --------------: | ---------------: | --------------------------: |
| Credit card          |          $2,000 |              24% |                         $80 |
| Personal loan        |          $3,000 |              12% |                        $220 |
| Loan from his sister |            $400 | 0%, by agreement |                         $50 |
| **Total**            |      **$5,400** |                  |                    **$350** |

The required payments use $350 of the money Sam has set aside, leaving him **$150 extra**: $500 − $350. He chooses the highest-rate approach, so that extra money goes to the card. Its payment becomes $230: the $80 required payment plus $150 extra. He pays $220 toward the loan and the agreed $50 to his sister, bringing the total paid to $500.

To see what those payments do, we'll calculate one month's interest on each lender's opening balance using the annual rate divided by 12. In this example, there are no fees or new purchases, both lenders allow the payments without a penalty, and the payments happen after interest is added. Your products may calculate interest differently, so use their statements when you do this with your own debt.

| Debt          | Opening balance | Interest added |  Payment | Closing balance |
| ------------- | --------------: | -------------: | -------: | --------------: |
| Credit card   |          $2,000 |            $40 |     $230 |          $1,810 |
| Personal loan |          $3,000 |            $30 |     $220 |          $2,810 |
| Sister        |            $400 |             $0 |      $50 |            $350 |
| **Total**     |      **$5,400** |        **$70** | **$500** |      **$4,970** |

So Sam sent out $500, but he doesn't owe $500 less. He owes $430 less because $70 of the payment covered interest. That's the difference we're looking for when we check the closing balance.

What if he'd chosen the smallest-balance approach instead? His sister would get $200 and his card would get $80. Under the same first-month assumptions, he'd still finish with $4,970 of total debt, but more of it would be on the card and less would be owed to his sister. Those different balances could lead to different interest costs later. We'd need to follow more than this one month to compare the full payoff.

Now suppose Sam's income fell to $2,700. With the same $2,400 costs and $100 reserve, he'd have $200 for $350 of required payments: a **$150 shortfall**, with nothing available for extra repayment. At that point, he needs to revisit the whole payment plan and contact the people he owes. Choosing between repayment methods won't cover the missing money.

## A tax bill or a collection notice [#a-tax-bill-or-a-collection-notice]

When a notice arrives, start by checking who sent it, how much it says you owe, and when you need to respond. Use official contact details to verify it, and keep both a copy of the notice and a record of your reply. Those details tell you what needs attention next.

If the bill is for **U.S. federal taxes**, the IRS offers payment plans and other help depending on your circumstances. You still need to file required returns even if you can't pay in full, and a payment plan may still carry interest or penalties. The IRS's current [tax-debt options](https://www.irs.gov/payments/get-help-with-tax-debt) and [payment guidance](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc202) explain the routes available. If you're elsewhere, use your own tax authority's process.

If someone calls to collect a debt, first verify the company before paying or sharing sensitive information. You need to know who the creditor is and how they arrived at the balance, so ask for those details. If you dispute an amount, keep it marked as disputed while you check it. [CFPB: checking a collector, U.S. guidance.](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-tell-if-a-debt-collector-is-legitimate-or-a-scam-en-1699/)

Under the **U.S. federal debt-collection rule**, covered collectors generally provide validation information that includes the debt details and a deadline for a 30-day dispute period. Pay attention to that deadline: a timely written dispute requires the collector to pause collection of the disputed amount until it responds as required. Read the notice alongside the CFPB's [validation guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-information-does-a-debt-collector-have-to-give-me-about-the-debt-en-331/) so you can follow the process that applies. This doesn't cover every creditor, and you shouldn't assume it applies outside the U.S.

Court papers need separate attention, so get local legal help promptly if you're dealing with a court deadline, threatened loss of housing, or an old or disputed claim. This chapter can help you organize the problem, but it can't set the legal order of your debts or decide whether a claim is enforceable.

## When the money is between people you know [#when-the-money-is-between-people-you-know]

If you borrow from a friend and say, “I'll sort you out,” what have you actually agreed to? You may mean when your next pay arrives, while your friend may be expecting the money on a particular date. You need to agree on the amount, the date, and what happens if your pay is late.

Start by agreeing whether the money is a gift or a loan. If it's a loan, write down the amount, any interest, the payment dates, and what you'll do if things change, then make sure each person has a copy. If you're the one lending, think through what would happen to your own bills if the payment came late or didn't come at all. You need that answer before saying yes. [CFPB: family lending and borrowing.](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/adult-financial-education/tips-for-managing-family-lending-and-borrowing/)

That's why Sam's sister is still in his plan even though she charges no interest. They agreed on $50, and choosing to put extra money toward the card doesn't change that agreement. If he needs to change what he pays her, they need another conversation.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Now we're going to do this with your debt. You'll use workbook **[page 13: My debt details](/docs/workbook/my-debt-details)** to understand the amounts, then **[page 14: My debt plan](/docs/workbook/my-debt-plan)** to decide what happens next. Two sheets of paper with the same headings will work just as well.

1. **Check each amount.** Your starting point is page 3, “What I owe.” Add the details that will help you plan: the creditor, balance date, purpose, rate, fees, required payment, due date, and any overdue or disputed amounts. Include collateral, rate changes, and early-payment terms so those conditions stay beside the balance. List anything you still need to find out.
2. **Mark urgent consequences.** For each payment, write what could happen if you miss it. Add any notices and deadlines, then decide whom you need to contact and by when. This is how you'll see what needs attention before choosing where extra money goes.
3. **Find the real payment amount.** Bring over Chapter 4's plan for the same period and show your non-debt needs, any reserve, required debt payments, and money left. Check that you've counted each payment once. If the result is negative, write down the shortfall and what you'll do about it; there isn't extra money to allocate yet.
4. **Choose a next step.** If you have affordable extra money, name the debt it will go toward and why. If you don't, write the next contact or income action instead. Give the action a date and record any agreement that has actually been confirmed, so you know what you can rely on.
5. **Check what changed.** Set a date to review the plan after payments. When you come back to it, record new charges, the payments you actually made, and the closing balances. If the debt grew, work out why before repeating the same plan.

On Sam's page 14, you would see $500 available for debt, with $350 needed for required payments and $150 extra going to the card. At his review, he compares the next statements with the $4,970 closing total from our simplified example. You'll make the same comparison using your own terms and dates.

If you have no debt, your answer can simply be “none checked today.” Keep the product questions for before you take on a new obligation; there's no need to borrow money just to complete an exercise.

# 1. Start where you are (/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are)



*First draft. The [source notes](#sources-and-draft-notes) are at the end.*

Before we talk about what to do with your money, let's get a clear picture of where you are. How much do you have right now, what money comes in, and how much do you owe? Those are the questions we're going to work through first.

You could have a job that pays a lot and still struggle to cover your bills. You could have no job and receive money from somewhere else. So when I ask where you are financially, telling me your job title only gives me part of the picture. We need to look at what happens to the money.

I know what it feels like to have debt with no job because I've been there. I lost my job during my honeymoon, and my wife and I moved to New York with debt from our wedding. Our living costs went up, my wife was a full-time student, and I didn't have a job. I spent a lot of time living on credit, which left me with more debt to work through. I'm still figuring my way out of that as I write this.

That's the place I'm speaking from. I have things I've learned that can help, and I also have my own numbers to deal with. We're going to start by looking at yours.

## Why I want you to put it on paper [#why-i-want-you-to-put-it-on-paper]

You need to see the numbers before you can make a plan with them. And I mean see them: open the account, look at the balance, and look at how much you owe. Write it on a sheet of paper and put it in front of you.

Talking about money can be uncomfortable, especially when you already know there's something you don't want to look at. But you can't finesse your way around the amount sitting in the account. “I have some savings” leaves us guessing; “I have $1,040” gives us a number we can use. The same goes for debt. Once you've written down what you owe, we can talk about what to do with it.

You don't have to solve the whole thing while you make the list. For now, get used to looking at the number and saying, “This is where I am today.” If you need to take a break, take one and come back. Then we can work through what money you have, which payment is coming up, and what needs to change.

By the end of this chapter, you'll have three lists: what you have, what comes in, and what you owe. You'll put their totals on one page and choose your starting path.

## Where does your money come from? [#where-does-your-money-come-from]

Let's sort income by where it comes from. We'll use four groups.

<figure className="not-prose my-8 rounded-xl border border-fd-border p-5">
  <figcaption className="mb-5 text-center font-semibold">
    Your income and support
  </figcaption>

  <ul className="grid list-none gap-4 p-0 sm:grid-cols-2">
    <li className="rounded-lg border border-fd-border border-t-4 border-t-fd-primary bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        1\. An employer pays you
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Hourly pay, salary, tips, commission, bonuses.
      </p>
    </li>

    <li className="rounded-lg border border-fd-border border-t-4 border-t-fd-primary bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        2\. You sell your own work
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Freelance work, services, products, a business you run.
      </p>
    </li>

    <li className="rounded-lg border border-fd-border border-t-4 border-t-fd-primary bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        3\. What you own pays you
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Interest, dividends, rent, royalties.
      </p>
    </li>

    <li className="rounded-lg border border-fd-border border-t-4 border-t-fd-primary bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        4\. You receive support or retirement payments
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Benefits, pensions, regular family support, child support.
      </p>
    </li>
  </ul>
</figure>

These are the groups we'll use to build your money plan. Tax forms may sort the same payments in other ways. The map draws on [official income definitions](/docs/research#income-map).

### 1. An employer pays you [#1-an-employer-pays-you]

If you work for someone who pays you, that money goes here. You might be an hourly cashier or a salaried engineer; hourly pay and salary describe how your pay is worked out, but both come from an employer. A sales worker's commission belongs here too when their employer pays it.

### 2. You sell your own work [#2-you-sell-your-own-work]

This is money from goods or services you sell through work you run yourself. You might cut hair, design websites, sell meals, or run a shop. If you make videos and earn money from ads or sponsors, that can go here too.

The money customers pay is your sales revenue. But running the business costs money, so we need to keep those costs beside the sales before deciding how much the work gives you.

### 3. What you own pays you [#3-what-you-own-pays-you]

You may receive interest on savings, dividends from shares, or rent from a property. You may also receive royalties when someone pays to use work or rights you own. The payment comes from something you own, which is why it has its own place on the page.

If “dividend” is a new word for you, it's a payment a company makes to its shareholders. You can receive a salary and dividends, but we'll record them in different groups so you can see where each payment came from.

### 4. You receive support or retirement payments [#4-you-receive-support-or-retirement-payments]

If you receive a pension, cash benefits, regular family support, or child support, put that money on the page too. Remember, we're trying to see what comes into your life, including money you receive when you don't have a job.

Keep any limits on how you can use the money beside the amount. If someone helps by providing free housing, write that beside the list as well. That help can reduce what you need to pay, even though it doesn't put cash in your account.

### What about streamers and people with more than one source? [#what-about-streamers-and-people-with-more-than-one-source]

You don't have to fit your whole working life into one box. Sort each payment by where it comes from, and use as many groups as you need.

| Money received                                               | Where it goes on this map |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| A salary from a company that employs you to make videos      | Employer                  |
| Ads, paid subscriptions, or sponsors for the channel you run | Own work                  |
| A dividend from shares you own                               | What you own              |
| Regular cash support from family with no repayment expected  | Support                   |
| An hourly job plus freelance design work                     | Employer **and** own work |

If you earn a salary, run a business, and receive dividends, all three belong on your page. We want to see each source, even when more than one applies to you.

You may come across a payment that seems to fit two groups, such as money from a rental business. Choose the description that best fits the payment and count it once. The same care applies if your own business pays you: adding the business's sales to your pay would make it look as though both amounts were separate personal income. If you're unsure where a payment belongs, write ‘to check’ beside it and keep going. We can come back to the group without losing track of the money.

## A deposit is not always new income [#a-deposit-is-not-always-new-income]

Suppose you move $500 from savings into your spending account. The $500 is now in a different place, but you haven't earned another $500. Borrowing that amount also puts cash in your account, except now you have $500 to repay.

We still need to see that cash because it can help cover a cost. Keep another line for money from selling things, drawing on savings, loans, and one-time gifts. Beside each amount, mark whether it can happen again and whether you have to pay it back. That way, we can tell what you received from what you expect to keep earning.

An investment sale gives us another reason to look at where a deposit came from. Let's say you bought an investment for $800 and sold it for $1,000. Ignoring fees and taxes, you gained $200, even though the sale put $1,000 in your account. The rest was money you had already put into the investment. These amounts are an example, not a promised return. [Source: Investor.gov's capital-gain definition](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/capital-gain).

Keep the gain beside the sale record so you can see what happened, but don't add it on top of the $1,000 you received. It's already part of that amount. And before you use the sale to plan next month's spending, remember that receiving the money once doesn't mean you'll receive it every month.

## What counts as debt? [#what-counts-as-debt]

Debt is money you owe. It might be money owed to a bank, the $200 you borrowed from a friend, or a bill you still need to pay. Even if nobody is charging interest, you still owe the money, so it belongs on the list.

We'll sort those amounts by how they came about.

<figure className="not-prose my-8 rounded-xl border border-fd-border p-5">
  <figcaption className="mb-5 text-center font-semibold">
    Money you owe
  </figcaption>

  <ul className="space-y-4 border-l-2 border-fd-border pl-4">
    <li className="list-none rounded-lg bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        You borrowed or used credit
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        From a lender, a friend, a relative, or a service that lets you buy now and pay later.
      </p>
    </li>

    <li className="list-none rounded-lg bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        You received something and still owe the bill
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Unpaid rent, utilities, medical care, or other goods and services.
      </p>
    </li>

    <li className="list-none rounded-lg bg-fd-card p-4">
      <p className="mb-2 font-semibold">
        You owe a tax, fine, or court-ordered payment
      </p>

      <p className="text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Taxes, fines, or court-ordered payments you owe.
      </p>
    </li>
  </ul>
</figure>

The groups help us find what you owe; we'll still need to look at the terms before deciding what to do about it. A home loan and money borrowed from a friend both go under borrowed money, for example, even though their costs, risks, and payment dates can be very different. [Debt definitions and examples](/docs/research#debt-map).

For now, we're looking for the amount you still owe today. That includes a mortgage or a card balance you intend to clear on the due date. Include bills you already owe even when they aren't late, and add the due dates if you know them. A purchase you're thinking about making doesn't belong here yet, because you haven't made it.

Follow how the debt came about when choosing its group. A student loan from the government is still borrowed money. If a court order concerns an existing debt, the order doesn't give you a second copy of that debt to count. The same goes for a loan you've used to pay off a bill: record the loan that's left, and take the paid bill out of your total. If you're disputing an amount, keep it on a separate line while you check it so it stays visible without getting mixed into the confirmed amounts.

### Is it good debt or bad debt? [#is-it-good-debt-or-bad-debt]

You may have a reason for thinking a debt was a good decision, and we can look at that. Calling it good doesn't change what you owe, though, so it still belongs on the page. To decide whether borrowing helped you, we need to know more than the label:

* What did it pay for?
* What will it cost?
* When must you pay it?
* Can you make those payments?
* What could you lose if you can't?

We'll work through those questions in [Chapter 5](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt). For now, include the amount even if you think borrowing it was a good choice.

## Find your starting path [#find-your-starting-path]

Now we can use what you've learned to find your starting path. First, do you have income or support coming in? An ongoing source counts even if the payments arrive at uneven times, but make a note if it may stop. If you're living from savings with no current income source, use the no-income row and record the savings beside it. You have money to work with, but we're keeping that separate from having more coming in.

Then ask whether you owe money. Those two answers give you one of the four starting points below.

| Your starting point                              | You owe money                 | You don't owe money               |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| **You have income or support coming in**         | **I-D** · Income with debt    | **I-ND** · Income without debt    |
| **You have no current income or support source** | **N-D** · No income with debt | **N-ND** · No income without debt |

These labels help you find the parts of the book that fit where you are today. We still need your lists to see whether your income covers your costs and how much cash you have saved. Two people in the same row can have very different amounts to work with.

### Four examples [#four-examples]

Here's how that works for four fictional people. The made-up amounts show one month's money coming in and the total debt each person still owes, so we're comparing the same things in each row.

| Example                                        | Money coming in                                                                                                | Money owed            | Path |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ---- |
| Sam has an hourly job and does freelance work. | $2,000 in take-home pay plus $300 from freelance work after business costs. Tax may still be due on that $300. | $200 owed to a friend | I-D  |
| Lee receives a pension.                        | $1,800                                                                                                         | $0                    | I-ND |
| Jo has no current income source.               | $0; living from savings                                                                                        | $600 on a card        | N-D  |
| Ari has no current income source.              | $0                                                                                                             | $0                    | N-ND |

You can see that Sam has more than one income source and Lee receives a pension. We can still place each of them using the same two questions: is money coming in, and do they owe money? The sources help us understand their situations without needing a new path for every combination.

## Your first worksheet [#your-first-worksheet]

If you have the companion workbook, turn to [page 1: What I have now](/docs/workbook/what-i-have). We'll use pages 1–4 for this chapter.

If you don't have the workbook, grab a notebook or some paper and a pen. I'll tell you what to write at each step, so you can do the whole exercise that way. A document you can keep open beside you works too if you can't or don't want to write by hand.

Write what you know, and if you don't know a number or a word yet, that's okay. Put “not sure yet” and keep going. We're getting a picture of where you are right now; you don't need every box filled in before you can move on. We'll work through the details as we go.

Put today's date at the top so you know when you made this picture of your money. Start with your own money, or, if you're making a shared household plan, use that same household for all three lists. Either way, each balance should appear only once.

### Step 1: Write down what you have now [#step-1-write-down-what-you-have-now]

Start with [workbook page 1: What I have now](/docs/workbook/what-i-have), or head your own sheet **“What I have now.”** Give each place you hold money its own line, with room beside it for the balance, the label used by the account, and the date you checked. Leave some space for notes too, including an available balance if the account shows one. We want to be able to tell where each number came from when we look back at the page.

Open each bank account you use, including your everyday account, savings, and any app that holds money for you. Count the cash in your wallet or at home too. Copy the balance you can see rather than rounding it or writing what you think is in there.

If all you have is an old statement, keep its amount and date as a note and mark the account “to check.” Find a current balance before including it in today's confirmed total. We want to know what's there now, not what was there the last time you looked.

Your app may show both a current balance and an available balance. Copy both with their labels, along with any pending payments, deposits, or transfers. Because transactions can take time to appear, check whether a payment is already included before subtracting it yourself. Otherwise, you could count the same payment twice. [Source: CFPB balance guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/bank-accounts/know-your-overdraft-options/).

When we add the accounts, we need one balance from each. Use the current balance if the account shows it; otherwise, use the balance you copied and keep its label. The available balance is extra information about that account, not extra money to add to it.

Add the confirmed positive balances to the cash you've counted and put the result beside **“Money I have now: $\_\_\_\_\_.”** If there's still an account to check, call this a partial total so you don't mistake it for the full picture. Keep notes about holds and money set aside for bills beside the result, because some of what you have is already needed for something.

As you add the accounts, check that you're counting each amount once. If an app displays your linked bank balance, you're looking at the same money in two places. A transfer between your own accounts also counts once.

Available credit and overdraft limits stay out of this total because they tell you what you could borrow. If an account is below zero, move the amount owed to your debt list. We'll account for it there; subtracting it from this cash total as well would count that debt twice.

You may also have investments, retirement accounts, property, or other assets. Give those a separate part of the sheet called **“Other things you own,”** where you record the value shown and its date, marking any estimate as an estimate. Keep them separate from money you can use now, and leave out balances you've already included in the cash list. We want to know about them without treating them as another copy of money you've counted.

If you can't find a number, “to check” is enough for now. Leave that note where you can see it until you find the record; writing zero would tell us something different.

### Step 2: List what comes in [#step-2-list-what-comes-in]

Next we want to see what came in over a month. Use [workbook page 2: What comes in](/docs/workbook/what-comes-in), or write **“What comes in”** on plain paper. Choose the month you're looking at and put it at the top, then use your pay records and accounts to give each source its own line. Beside the source, write its group and the amount you received. Our examples use generic $ amounts; use one currency when adding your own figures.

Leave room to note the next payment, whether the amount varies, and any costs or tax still to cover. You can come back to those details if you don't know them yet. For employer pay, record what reached you after payroll deductions. For your own work or rental income, subtract the costs you know, then keep a note of costs or tax you still need to cover. Put “not sure yet” beside anything you haven't worked out. That note needs to stay beside the total so you don't plan as though every dollar is free to spend.

Below the income list, give other cash from savings, sales, gifts, or borrowing its own line. Write the amount, whether you must pay it back, and whether it was a one-time receipt. If someone paid a bill for you, note that help separately too. This lets you see what helped you through the month without assuming it will all happen again next month.

Now add the income entries for your chosen month and write **“Income and support received during \_\_\_\_\_: $\_\_\_\_\_.”** Keep the costs and tax still to cover beside the result, with other cash receipts on their own line. Keep this total separate from today's account balance as well. If your pay is already in the account, it's already included in that balance; the monthly income total tells us how much came in during the period.

### Step 3: List what you owe [#step-3-list-what-you-owe]

Now turn to [workbook page 3: What I owe](/docs/workbook/what-i-owe), or start a sheet headed **“What I owe.”** For each debt, give yourself a line for who you owe, what it's for, the amount still owed, and the date you checked it. Leave room beside that for any payment details you know.

Go through your card and loan accounts, gather your unpaid bills, and check for taxes or money borrowed from people. As you copy each balance and the date you checked it, make sure you're taking the amount still owed. A monthly payment only tells us what you're paying at a time; it doesn't tell us the size of the whole debt.

Payment dates, interest, fees, and terms are optional for now. If you know the next payment and its date, write them down, and add any interest or fees you know about. If you don't, leave the space blank or write “not sure yet.” I don't want you getting stuck on a term you haven't learned yet when you can already write down who you owe and how much.

We'll go through interest and fees in [Chapter 5: Make a plan for debt](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt) and [Chapter 6: Credit cards](/docs/chapters/credit-cards). Right now, we're putting what you owe in one place so you can see it.

Keep your business's debts on a separate list, making a note to check any you may be responsible for yourself. If you know who you owe but can't find the balance, include the name and put “not sure yet” beside it. That gives you something to follow up without having to guess the amount.

Add the balances you've confirmed and put the result beside **“Money I owe: $\_\_\_\_\_.”** Keep disputed or unknown amounts beside it so you can see what still needs checking. If any balance is missing, call the result a partial total. The missing amount isn't zero; it just isn't part of what you've confirmed yet.

### Step 4: Put the whole page in front of you [#step-4-put-the-whole-page-in-front-of-you]

Bring those three lists to [workbook page 4: My money today](/docs/workbook/my-money-today), or start a fresh sheet called **“My money today.”** We can now put the totals beside each other and see what they tell us. In this made-up example, all balances were checked on the same day and there are no pending transactions.

<div className="not-prose my-8 rounded-lg border border-fd-border bg-fd-card p-6">
  <p className="mb-1 text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
    Example sheet · made-up amounts
  </p>

  <p className="mb-5 text-xl font-semibold">
    My money today
  </p>

  <dl className="space-y-5">
    <div className="border-b border-fd-border pb-4">
      <dt className="font-semibold">
        Money I have now: $1,040
      </dt>

      <dd className="mt-1 text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Everyday account $600 + savings $400 + cash $40.
      </dd>
    </div>

    <div className="border-b border-fd-border pb-4">
      <dt className="font-semibold">
        Income received last month: $2,300
      </dt>

      <dd className="mt-1 text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Take-home pay. Some of this is already in the account balance above.
      </dd>
    </div>

    <div className="border-b border-fd-border pb-4">
      <dt className="font-semibold">
        Money I owe: $4,200
      </dt>

      <dd className="mt-1 text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Card $3,000 + loan $1,000 + friend $200.
      </dd>
    </div>

    <div>
      <dt className="font-semibold">
        Other things I own: listed separately
      </dt>

      <dd className="mt-1 text-sm text-fd-muted-foreground">
        Values and estimates stay on their own list.
      </dd>
    </div>
  </dl>
</div>

The money on hand, the month's income, and the debt are now on one page, but they still tell us different things. Adding all three wouldn't give you a useful total. We want to be able to look from one to the other and understand where you are.

Use page 4 or your own sheet to bring your results together:

1. Start with today's date and whose money you're listing, so it's clear whether this is your own picture or a shared household picture.
2. Bring across **“Money I have now”** and the total from your first list. Bring its notes too: any missing accounts, holds, pending items, and money set aside. Keep other things you own on their separate list so they don't get mixed into this amount.
3. Add **“Income and support received”** with the month and its total. Alongside it, include your current sources and any costs, tax, or amounts you still need to check. That lets you see what came in without losing the details that affect how you can use it.
4. Add **“Money I owe”** and its total, with unknown or disputed amounts beside it. As you copy all three totals, keep the word “partial” on any that have missing amounts; moving a number to a new page shouldn't make those gaps disappear.
5. Use the income and debt answers to write your starting path. If you know the next bill or payment, put it beside that path, along with one number or term you want to come back to. You'll have a place to begin when you pick up the page again.

Okay, put the pen down for a moment and look at the page. You can see what you have, what comes in, and what you owe, along with the things you still need to check. That's enough to give us somewhere to start. Keep adding to it as you find the missing amounts; a few boxes left blank don't stop you from taking the next step.

Keep this sheet somewhere you can return to and update when your situation changes. We'll use it to work through spending and payment dates in [Chapter 4](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid).

Find your row below to see which chapter to use next. You can work on what fits your situation now and come back for the rest as things change.

# 2. The life you want (/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want)



*First draft. Based on [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) and [Note 4](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-4). Sources and example assumptions are at the end.*

Okay, so you've put your money on paper. You can see what you have, what comes in, and what you owe. Now where are you trying to go?

Sometimes I look at a decision and wonder, what was the plan? What were you trying to get to? It baffles me how you can put so much effort into something without knowing what you want it to give you. That's why I think we need to spend some time on this question before we start talking about earning more money.

You might want to travel, get home in time to eat with your family, or look at your bank account without worrying about whether the bills are covered. All of those are things we can work towards, but “I want more money” doesn't tell us which one matters to you. We need to get specific enough to picture the life, estimate what it costs, and choose something to work on next.

## Start with an ordinary day [#start-with-an-ordinary-day]

Let's work backwards from where you'd love to be five or ten years from now, or a nearer date if that fits what you're working on. I mean getting into the details of an ordinary day: where you live, what time you wake up, and what happens once you're out of bed.

Let's say you want to get up at 5:30, go to the gym, and come home while your partner is getting the kids ready for school. You drop them off on the way to work, do your job, and get home in time to have dinner with your family every day. That might be exactly what you want. Now we have something to work with, because we can start asking what it would take to have that day.

Some of it will cost money, and some of it will need your time. Where would you have to live? How far could you travel to work and still make it home? Write about those things along with the people you want to spend time with and what you want your evenings to look like.

Of course, you might not want kids, or you might love the job you already have. You may want more time to look after someone. That's fine. Write the life you want, including the responsibilities you want to keep, so we're working towards something that matters to you.

## Be honest about what matters to you [#be-honest-about-what-matters-to-you]

Maybe you care about cars, or you want to buy nice clothes. Maybe you don't care about any of that and just want to travel. People want different things, and I don't think we should be shaming someone because their idea of a good life is different from ours. You don't have to become a millionaire to have a goal worth working towards.

But give me the whole picture. If being there for your kids matters to you, put that beside the car you want to drive. Otherwise, we could choose an income goal, find work that pays it, and discover that the hours keep you away from the very thing you wanted the money for.

Once you've written it down, decide what matters most and what you could change. The school pickup might matter more than the car, or you might still want the car but be fine waiting longer for it. Knowing that gives you some room to make decisions when we work out the cost.

## Put a cost beside the life [#put-a-cost-beside-the-life]

Now we can put some amounts beside that life. First decide whether you're planning for your own money or for the household, and use the same choice throughout. If someone else will cover part of a shared cost, write down how much and whether you've agreed on it. We need to know whose money pays for which part.

Start with costs you already know from your bills and account records. For something you don't pay for yet, find a current price and check what it includes. You're allowed to estimate; just write “estimate” beside the amount. If you don't know, put “not sure yet” and come back to it. Leaving a cost out would make the life look cheaper without making it any cheaper to live.

Include home costs, food, transport, care, health, giving, and the things you enjoy, along with payments you still expect to owe. If part of your goal is to have money saved, that also needs a place in the monthly plan. We'll include less frequent costs too, so the bills that arrive once a year don't disappear from the calculation.

### Give every amount a time period [#give-every-amount-a-time-period]

A monthly bill can go straight in the monthly column. If a recurring cost is $2,400 a year, divide it by 12 and put its $200 monthly share there. Keep the actual due date beside it, because spreading the amount across a calculation doesn't change when someone expects you to pay.

One-time costs need their own list. If the life you described means moving, for example, you may need money up front as well as the new monthly rent. Write down the cost, what you've already set aside for it, and how many months you have left to save the rest.

Suppose the goal costs $6,000 and you've already saved $1,200. That leaves $4,800, which comes to $200 a month over 24 months, without assuming any interest. Put that $200 inside your monthly saving total once. Now you can see how the one-time goal affects the amount you need each month.

### Use money you can plan with [#use-money-you-can-plan-with]

When you compare the cost of that life with what you earn, use money you can plan with. If an employer pays you, that's your take-home pay after taxes and other payroll deductions. Gross pay is the amount before those deductions, so using it here would leave you planning to spend money that doesn't all reach you.

If costs or tax still need to come out, use the notes you made in Chapter 1 to account for them first. If you don't know the tax amount, keep the comparison marked as incomplete until you check it. There's no single percentage we can guess for everybody, and this exercise won't calculate how much salary or business sales would produce your take-home target.

As you do that, check you're only counting each cost once. A car payment listed under transport shouldn't appear again under debt payments, and health insurance already deducted from your pay shouldn't be subtracted again. The total balance you owe also stays separate from the amount you plan to pay this month.

## Let's walk through Michelle's plan [#lets-walk-through-michelles-plan]

Let's say Michelle works in customer service and takes home $3,000 a month. She wants to spend her working day thinking, researching, and writing, and she wants to take her kids to school and be available when they need her. If the school calls, being able to show up matters to her. She doesn't want her work to get in the way of that.

She'd also like to drive a Range Rover, have some help cleaning the house, and save money each month. She doesn't care as much about travel, so that gets less of her budget. Those are her choices; your list may look completely different.

Michelle and the amounts in this example are fictional. We'll assume her partner has agreed to contribute $2,400 a month to the household plan and that the money is available. If you're making your own shared plan, check that contribution together before building the rest around it.

**All amounts below are made-up planning assumptions in generic dollars, not local price quotes.**

| Part of Michelle's chosen life | Monthly amount | What this example includes                                                                 |
| ------------------------------ | -------------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Home                           |         $2,200 | Rent, utilities, phone, and internet                                                       |
| Food and household supplies    |           $600 | Groceries and everyday supplies                                                            |
| Transport                      |         $1,100 | An assumed $800 car payment plus $300 for fuel, insurance, and maintenance                 |
| Health and care                |           $400 | Costs not already deducted from pay, including planned care for the children               |
| Cleaning help                  |           $800 | A chosen monthly allowance; no weekly price or frequency is implied                        |
| Gym, clothes, and hobbies      |           $200 | Chosen personal spending                                                                   |
| Giving and gifts               |           $100 | This household's chosen amount                                                             |
| Less frequent costs            |           $200 | $2,400 a year for items not counted above, such as school costs and a small trip           |
| Other debt payments            |           $300 | Existing payments, excluding the car payment already listed                                |
| Saving                         |         $2,500 | $200 for the moving goal below and $2,300 for other saving goals, including a cash reserve |
| **Total monthly target**       |     **$8,400** | **The household amount needed for these assumptions**                                      |

Her moving goal uses the $6,000 example we just worked through. With $1,200 set aside and 24 months to save the remaining $4,800, she needs $200 a month. We've already included that in the $2,500 saving row, so don't add it on top of the $8,400.

We're putting a cost on a future version of Michelle's life here; her spending today may look very different. The table assumes no further up-front purchase costs, which she'd need to check against an actual car quote or move. She'd also need to check each allowance before committing to it. For now, these amounts let us work through the decision.

## Now we can see the gap [#now-we-can-see-the-gap]

With a household target of **$8,400 a month** and her partner's assumed contribution of **$2,400**, Michelle needs to bring in **$6,000 a month** after deductions and any costs or tax still to cover. Her current take-home pay is **$3,000**, so the difference she needs to work on is **$3,000 a month**.

Okay, now she has something to work with. She can look at ways to earn more, change part of the life she's priced, or give herself longer to get there. She may also check one of those estimates and find that it was wrong. That's a reason to work through the number again, not to throw away the whole plan.

And remember why she started. If she finds a way to bring in $6,000 but can never do the school pickup, she still has a decision to make. She wanted to be available for her children. We can't forget that just because the income reaches the number on the page.

The $2,500 saving choice belongs to Michelle's example; it isn't an amount everyone needs to save. Even if she reaches her monthly income target, she still has to set the money aside over time before her moving fund is ready.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Now try that with the life you described. Workbook pages [5: My chosen life](/docs/workbook/my-chosen-life), [6: What that life costs](/docs/workbook/what-that-life-costs), and [7: My target and next step](/docs/workbook/my-target-and-next-step) give you space to work through it. If you're using plain paper, use the same page names and follow these steps.

1. **Describe the day.** Start with your name or household, today's date, and the date you're working towards. Then write about your morning, your work or other responsibilities, your evening, and your time off. Give yourself enough detail to see what you want your days to look like. As you read it back, mark what matters most and what you'd be willing to change, because those choices will help when you see the cost.
2. **List the costs.** Beside each part of the life you want, write an amount, how often you'd pay it, its monthly share, and where the estimate came from. Use one currency throughout so you can add the figures. Include saving and payments you expect to owe, and note who would cover any shared costs. If you don't know an amount yet, leave that gap visible rather than letting it disappear from the plan.
3. **List the one-time goals.** For each goal, write the full cost, the money already set aside for it, what you still need, and how many months are left. If you've already set aside enough, you have zero left to find. Otherwise, divide what you still need by the months left and include that monthly amount in saving once. Check which money you've assigned to each goal; the same savings can't fund two things at once. If you don't know the cost or timing, mark the result incomplete. And if the goal is due now, write down the immediate shortfall. There are no months left to spread it across, so dividing by zero won't help you plan for it.
4. **Compare like with like.** Add your monthly costs, payments, and saving to get the target. Beside it, put income and support for the same person or household and the same period, allowing for known costs and tax still to cover. If your income is uneven, use a range from your records so you're looking at more than your best month. Now subtract that income from the target. A positive result shows the gap; a negative result means the listed income is more than the estimated target. Keep any missing costs and payment dates beside the comparison, because that result doesn't settle them.
5. **Choose one next step.** Look over what you've written and choose one number to check or one change to explore. Give that action a date, then set a date to review the whole page too. Prices and your circumstances can change, so you'll need to come back to the estimate as you learn more. We aren't fixing the next ten years of your life on this sheet.

You can stop with a partial plan if you've written down what you still need to find out. You don't need to invent a number just to fill the page. Keep the gaps visible so you know what to come back and check.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

If you have no current income or support, finding income is the next priority. Keep the life you described, but don't wait until every future estimate is finished before taking that step. You have things to pay for now too.

| Your path                     | Next chapter                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| I-D · Income with debt        | [4. When you get paid](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid), to plan the money coming in.                                        |
| I-ND · Income without debt    | [3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), to consider how your income and work fit the life you chose. |
| N-D · No income with debt     | [3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), to focus on an income source.                                |
| N-ND · No income without debt | [3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), to focus on an income source.                                |

Keep this page with the picture of your current money. You can now look at where you are and where you want to go together. Finishing the exercise doesn't mean you have to change jobs or start a business; the next chapter for your path will help you work through what to do from here.

The 5:30 morning and family sequence come from [Note 3's ordinary-day example](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3); the opening reaction about having a plan comes from [Note 4 around 01:00](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-4), after the abandoned wife anecdote, which remains omitted.
