# 4. When you get paid (/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid)



**First draft · Chapter 4.**

Okay, so you've been paid. What happens next?

My mom used to tell me that when I got paid, I should pay myself first. Put something away for myself. I think there's value in that, because you can spend the whole month working, get paid, pay everybody else, and reach the end with nothing saved. Then you do the same thing again the next month. I want us to make room for a saving habit where we can.

But there's a planning step before we decide how much to put away. We need to know what your money has to cover and when those payments are due. Otherwise, I could tell you to save a percentage that sounds great, and you'd be sitting there wondering how you're supposed to pay your rent.

That's the plan we're making here. It works for wages, business income, retirement payments, or support. If nothing is coming in right now, use the money you actually have and the shortfall section below. Don't wait for a future payday to see what needs attention.

## Look at the bills before the payday [#look-at-the-bills-before-the-payday]

Before the next payday, sit down with your statements, bills, and the money picture from Chapter 1. Look at the whole coming month, including the bills that won't leave your account for a few weeks. Then look a little further ahead. If this month's pay has to cover next month's rent, that rent belongs in the plan you're making now.

For each cost, write how much you need, when it's due, and when you need to send the payment for it to arrive on time. Start with the food, housing, utilities, transport, care, insurance, and required debt payments that apply to your life. Use the bill or agreement in front of you rather than assuming the amount is the same as last month, especially with something like a card minimum.

Some costs won't show up on this month's bills, but you still need to get ready for them. If you're putting a little aside each payday for an annual bill, write down what that money is for. Otherwise, you could look at the account, think you have money left over, and spend what you were keeping for that bill.

Then look at the subscriptions, dinners, trips, and other things you choose to spend on. You can care about those things; just be honest about what belongs where. Netflix doesn't become as urgent as rent because you enjoy watching it. You might need a phone or a car for work, but that still leaves a decision about which one you can afford.

This is why I want you to look at the whole period. You don't want to pay for your gym and streaming subscriptions because the money is there today, then discover you can't cover rent because it comes out later. The order the payments leave your account shouldn't make that decision for you. The [CFPB cash-flow tool](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/documents/7174/cfbp_your-money-your-goals_adjust_cash_flow_tool_2018-11_ADA.pdf) gives a way to map the dates; it is a US consumer-education resource.

## Know which money you're planning with [#know-which-money-youre-planning-with]

Before we add anything up, decide which cash you can use for this plan. If you've protected some savings for another purpose, leave that money out. If a payment is on its way but hasn't cleared yet, mark the amount as committed. We're trying to see what you can still make decisions with, so check that the same balance hasn't ended up in two places.

Put future receipts on a separate list with their expected dates, and distinguish a confirmed payment from one you're only hoping for. A customer saying they'll pay helps you plan, but you still need to check what actually arrives before spending it. We'll come back to that in Chapter 8, because spending a payment before it turns up is something I've fallen into myself.

If the money comes from your own work, it may still have business costs and tax to cover. Separate those amounts before deciding what's available for your personal spending. In the US, independent contractors may need to make estimated tax payments, so check the current official guidance for your situation. The saving percentages we'll use below don't tell you how much tax to set aside. [IRS gig-work tax guidance](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/manage-taxes-for-your-gig-work).

Keep using whichever source labels fit: **Employer, Own work, Assets, and Support / retirement.** You can have more than one. Help that doesn't arrive as cash still matters, but keep it separate from money you can spend. And if you're drawing from savings to get through this period, show that withdrawal without counting it as a new ongoing income source.

## Give saving a place in the plan [#give-saving-a-place-in-the-plan]

Once you've seen what the money needs to cover, you can decide what to put away and what you're saving for. What I care about here is getting into the habit of keeping some of what you earn, when your circumstances allow it. Saving doesn't have to wait until you feel like you're making a lot of money.

If you can afford to put away 25% to 30% of your pay, that's an amount I'd consider. But I mean if you can afford it. If that leaves you short for food or rent, the percentage doesn't work for you. You might start much smaller, and there will be periods when you can't put anything away. That's why we looked at the bills first.

You can start with a small amount that fits your circumstances; the CFPB's emergency-fund guide takes that approach too. If you set up an automatic saving transfer, keep an eye on the account it comes from. You don't want the transfer to go through when there isn't enough there and cause an overdraft. [CFPB emergency-saving guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/).

Let's use a fictional monthly plan in generic dollars. You bring home $5,000, and there are no further business costs or taxes to take out. All your required costs and debt payments come to $2,500, including money you need to reserve for later known bills. We'll leave giving out of this first version and work through it separately below.

| Monthly plan                   |  Amount |
| ------------------------------ | ------: |
| Take-home income               |  $5,000 |
| Required costs and payments    | −$2,500 |
| Saving: 25% of the full $5,000 | −$1,250 |
| Left to allocate               |  $1,250 |

Now you can see what the last $1,250 is available for. You might use some for dinners or other things you enjoy, put more toward debt, or keep more aside. Make that choice while you're looking at the whole plan, so the money doesn't disappear through purchases you never thought about together. You don't have to use it all up.

Now suppose the fictional numbers are tighter: you have $2,000 after tax, and required costs take $1,600 of it. With $400 left, you could choose to save 25% of **that $400 remainder**. That puts $100 into savings and leaves $300 for you to allocate. Measured against the original $2,000, you're saving 5%, even though you used 25% when you worked out what to keep from the remainder.

Notice what changed: in the first example, we saved a percentage of the whole take-home amount. In the second, we saved a percentage of what remained after required costs. Saying “I save 25%” doesn't tell us which one you mean. Write the dollar amount beside the percentage so you can see what the decision leaves you with.

If you have costly debt as well as room to save, compare those uses of the money in Chapter 5. The example here doesn't settle the right balance for everyone.

## Where giving fits for me [#where-giving-fits-for-me]

I'm a Christian, and I believe in paying my tithes. That's part of how I handle my money, and it's part of what I'm sharing with you here. I'm not going to spend this section arguing back and forth about that belief. What I can explain is the way I've made room for it in my own planning.

For a long time, I've found it easier to treat that 10% as already set aside and plan with the rest. If I'm planning to tithe, I don't want to finish allocating all my money and then remember that I still have my tithes to pay. I've also tithed on income before tax. The example here uses take-home income, so you can see exactly what we're calculating.

With $5,000 in take-home income, that 10% is $500, leaving $4,500 for the rest of the plan. You've still earned $5,000; you've decided that $500 of it is going toward giving. Thinking about the remainder from the start is what helps me account for it.

Here's one way the rest could work. This is a separate illustrative version, with saving chosen as 25% of the **$4,500 after giving**.

| Monthly plan with giving        |  Amount |
| ------------------------------- | ------: |
| Take-home income                |  $5,000 |
| Giving: 10% of take-home income |   −$500 |
| Required costs and payments     | −$2,500 |
| Saving: 25% of $4,500           | −$1,125 |
| Left to allocate                |    $875 |

Because we're now saving a percentage of the amount after giving, the saving amount changes too. We have to work through the whole plan again; we can't add a giving line and assume the same remainder will still be there.

If giving is part of your life, put it on the page alongside the bills so you can see what the whole plan asks of your money. This example has room for all of those choices. Yours may not, and if there's a gap, we need to acknowledge it and work through the shortfall section below. Choosing a giving or saving percentage won't make the missing money appear.

## A month can work while a week doesn't [#a-month-can-work-while-a-week-doesnt]

Let's go back to the first $5,000 plan, without giving. Suppose it arrives in two payments of $2,500, on the 1st and 15th. There is no opening balance assigned to this plan. Assume $2,000 of the required costs fall before the second payment, and $500 after it.

If you divide the monthly saving amount in half and take $625 out of that first payment, you'll have $1,875 left for $2,000 of bills. You're $125 short before the next payday, even though the monthly plan looked fine. This is why knowing the total isn't enough: we need to know when the money arrives and when it has to leave.

One possible schedule is:

| Period         |                         Money available | What this part covers                                       |                       Carried forward |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------: | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------: |
| 1st–14th       |                         $2,500 received | $2,000 required costs; hold the rest                        |                                  $500 |
| 15th–month end | $500 carried + $2,500 received = $3,000 | $500 required costs; $1,250 saving; $1,250 left to allocate | $0 unassigned after those allocations |

When the second payment arrives, the table gives every dollar somewhere to go. That doesn't mean you send it all out on the 15th. Keep each amount until you need it, and look ahead to what comes due before you're paid again. This example assumes the next payment arrives before the next period's costs; if your dates work differently, you'll need to reserve money for those costs now.

Your own calendar needs the actual date of each bill. Start with the opening balance, add a receipt when it comes in, subtract a payment when it goes out, and carry what's left to the next date. You're following the money through the month. If that running amount goes below zero, you've found a gap that the monthly total may have hidden. The [CFPB cash-flow worksheet](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/documents/10038/cfpb_creating-cash-flow-budget_tool_2021-08.pdf) uses this running-balance approach.

On workbook page 11, you can also subtract money when you reserve it for a bill. If you use that option, the running amount tells you what's still available for this plan, which can differ from the balance your bank shows. When the reserved bill is paid, don't subtract it again. You've already accounted for that money.

If the same dates keep clashing, contact the provider and ask whether a different due date or payment arrangement is available. If they offer a change, find out the new amount, any cost, when it starts, and what you still owe in the meantime. Keep planning around the existing date until the change is confirmed. Canceling and restarting a service doesn't generally resolve a bill you've already incurred. [CFPB guidance on adjusting cash flow](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/documents/7174/cfbp_your-money-your-goals_adjust_cash_flow_tool_2018-11_ADA.pdf).

## What if there isn't enough? [#what-if-there-isnt-enough]

Sometimes you do all of this and there still isn't enough to pay every bill. I'm not going to sit here and tell you that you should always be able to make it work, because I've been in that situation myself. And if there isn't room to save the percentage we just talked about, that's okay. We need to deal with the money you have.

When I'm in that position, I make a priority list. I look at what absolutely needs attention and what happens if I can't pay it. Your list might be different from mine, so write the consequences beside the amounts and dates. That gives you a reason for the order you choose, beyond whichever bill happens to arrive first.

Think about your basic needs and what protects your housing, health, and ability to earn. Include essential insurance and court-ordered obligations as you look at what could happen if a payment is missed. The dates and consequences in your own situation will help you decide what comes first. For bills you can't cover, contact the providers to ask what help or arrangements are available. The [CFPB prioritizing-bills tool](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_prioritizing-bills_tool.pdf) works through those consequences rather than giving everybody the same fixed order.

Here's a fictional shortfall for one pay period. You have $1,200 available, after any amounts already committed elsewhere. Needs and required payments total $1,500. There are no optional purchases, giving, or new saving in these figures. You're $300 short.

There isn't a saving percentage that makes those numbers fit. Use the shortfall sheet to see which bills are due and what is at risk, then check available support and contact the providers you can't pay in full. Record what they confirm, including any change to the amount or date. Until confirmed help or an agreed change closes it, that $300 gap is still there. Expected income needs to arrive before you can use it.

Keep any missed payment on your debt record, even if you had a more urgent bill to pay first. You'll still need to deal with what remains unpaid. If your housing or utilities are at immediate risk, or you have a court deadline, seek appropriate local help promptly so you can work with the rules and options where you live.

## Choose tools that help you use the plan [#choose-tools-that-help-you-use-the-plan]

Paper, a spreadsheet, or an app can all give you somewhere to keep this plan. Choose something you can use to see the amounts and dates together, because that's the information you need when you're deciding what to pay.

Suppose an app shows you $500, but you need $450 of it for a bill. You still need to be able to see that commitment when deciding what to spend. Check whether the app includes upcoming payments and whether its transactions are up to date. It can help you keep the records together, but you still have to decide what that money will cover.

The account you use needs to work with that plan too. Look at how you can access your money and make payments, what support is available, and what fees you could pay. Read the conditions for avoiding monthly charges instead of assuming the account will always be free. As the CFPB explains, some US accounts require things such as a minimum balance or direct deposit to avoid a fee. [CFPB account-fee guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/why-am-i-being-charged-a-monthly-maintenance-fee-for-my-bank-or-credit-union-account-en-2151/).

Also check who actually holds the money and what protection applies. In the US, some nonbank services place money at banks, where it may qualify for what's called pass-through FDIC deposit insurance. That coverage depends on requirements being met, so the app's appearance alone doesn't tell you whether your money qualifies. Read the disclosures. [FDIC explanation](https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/2023-07/my-money-insured-fdic). Other countries have different systems.

## Your turn [#your-turn]

Now let's do this with your money. Use workbook **[10. My next payment plan](/docs/workbook/my-next-payment-plan)**, **[11. My bill calendar](/docs/workbook/my-bill-calendar)**, and **[12. When money falls short](/docs/workbook/when-money-falls-short)**. If you're using plain paper, give three sheets those same headings and work through the steps below.

1. **Choose the period you're planning for.** Put the start and end dates at the top, along with the currency and whose money you're including. Write the cash available at the start, showing what you've left out because it's reserved elsewhere. List future receipts separately with their dates and how certain they are. Account for any business costs or tax still to cover once, so you can see what you're starting with and what still has to arrive.
2. **Give that money somewhere to go.** Bring your required costs, debt payments, and amounts reserved for later bills onto the page. Then include any giving, saving, and other spending you've chosen. If you use a percentage, write what you're taking that percentage of. An unknown amount means the plan is provisional; keep it visible so you know what to check before relying on the remainder.
3. **Follow it through the calendar.** Put each receipt and payment on its date, including automatic payments already set up. Allow enough time for a payment to arrive where it's due. Add money in, subtract money out, and carry the balance to the next date, marking whether incoming money has arrived or is still forecast. Now you can see whether the plan works all the way through the period.
4. **Work through any gap.** If the balance goes below zero or a need remains uncovered, take it to page 12. Write what could happen, whom you'll contact, what changes they've confirmed, and what remains unpaid. Go back through your choices before treating any remainder as money you can spend.
5. **Check the plan when you're paid.** Compare what actually arrived with what you expected, and confirm the bills before making payments or transfers. Make only those the available funds can support, then record what you did. Review the plan before the next payment comes in, or sooner if something changes.

If you move money between two accounts included in your calendar, label it as a transfer. Count the amount leaving one and entering the other once each; your combined balance hasn't changed. You haven't earned new income or paid a second expense. Money you've allocated to savings still belongs to you, but you've already chosen a purpose for it, so keep it out of the unassigned spending amount.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

| Your path                  | Next chapter                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

| N-D · No income, with debt | [3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), while acting on urgent shortfalls and provider contacts now.          |

# Book plan (/docs/outline)



## What the book does [#what-the-book-does]

Help the reader describe the life they want and calculate what it takes. Then help them make the next money decision from where they are. Growing income and reducing debt support that goal. This follows the correction in [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3).

The book is used by situation. Chapter numbers help readers find and return to a section; they do not require reading every page in order.

## The companion workbook [#the-companion-workbook]

Keep explanations, stories, examples, and exercise instructions in the book. Put the blank tables and answer spaces in the optional [companion workbook](/docs/workbook). Reference each workbook page by number and name. Readers without it must be able to follow the same steps on plain paper.

Chapter 1 uses workbook pages 1–4: What I have now, What comes in, What I owe, and My money today. Chapter 2 uses pages 5–7: My chosen life, What that life costs, and My target and next step. Chapter 3 uses pages 8–9: My income options and My next income step. Chapter 4 uses pages 10–12; Chapter 5 uses 13–14; Chapter 6 uses 15–16; Chapter 7 uses 17; Chapter 8 uses 18. Add later workbook pages as their chapter exercises are drafted. These are working page numbers; confirm the final references during print layout.

## The chapter plan [#the-chapter-plan]

Keep [Before we start](/docs/chapters/before-we-start) and [How to use this book](/docs/chapters/how-to-use-this-book) as short opening sections. The numbered chapters begin with a map of the reader's money.

### Find your place [#find-your-place]

* **[1. Start where you are](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are)** — Put what you have, what comes in, and what you owe on paper. Choose your starting path.
* **[2. The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want)** — Describe the life you want and put a cost on it.

### Build your money plan [#build-your-money-plan]

* **[3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income)** — Choose the next income step that fits your situation.
* **[4. When you get paid](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid)** — Make a plan for the next money that comes in.
* **[5. Make a plan for debt](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt)** — Understand what you owe and build a repayment plan.

### Use credit and spend [#use-credit-and-spend]

* **[6. Credit cards 101](/docs/chapters/credit-cards)** — Understand the card, the bill, and the payment decision.
* **[7. Credit scores 101](/docs/chapters/credit-scores)** — Know what a credit score can tell you and when it matters.
* **[8. Before you buy](/docs/chapters/before-you-buy)** — Decide whether an expensive purchase fits your plan.

### Protect and grow [#protect-and-grow]

* **[9. When life changes](/docs/chapters/when-life-changes)** — Adjust the plan when income, costs, or family needs change.
* **[10. The promise of fast money](/docs/chapters/fast-money)** — Examine a promise of quick wealth before acting on it.
* **[11. Before you invest](/docs/chapters/before-you-invest)** — Work out what the money is for and what risk you can take.
* **[12. Ways to invest](/docs/chapters/ways-to-invest)** — Understand the main investment choices and compare them.

## Drafted chapters [#drafted-chapters]

[Chapter 1: Start where you are](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) is drafted. It explains why seeing the numbers makes planning possible. It defines income and debt, shows the two money maps, explains mixed sources, and gives four starting-path examples. The exercise has readers check accounts and records, write what they have and owe, and put those totals beside income on one sheet. The book keeps the filled-in example and paper instructions. [Companion workbook pages 1–4](/docs/workbook) hold the blank worksheets.

[Chapter 2: The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want) now has a first draft, a rebuilt fictional Michelle example, workbook pages 5–7, and a [spoken adaptation](/docs/scripts/the-life-you-want). [Chapter 3: Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income) has a first draft, workbook pages 8–9, and a [spoken adaptation](/docs/scripts/grow-your-income). [Chapters 4–8](/docs/chapters) now also have first drafts, [spoken scripts](/docs/scripts), and workbook pages 10–18. [Chapters 9–12](/docs/chapters) remain placeholders with section plans and material to draw from. The title and final wording of the book's promise remain open.

The [October 1 incorporation plan](/docs/writing-plan) maps passages, proposed script outlines, exercises, drafting order, and checks still needed. Chapters 2–8 are developed as first drafts from this batch. The recording-based drafting sequence is complete; the drafts still need author review and final print layout.

Keep the existing chapter order and companion-workbook approach while these ideas are developed. Raw numerical examples and product claims still need the checks in [Research notes](/docs/research#recording-research-queue).

## Reader paths and money maps [#reader-paths-and-money-maps]

The four paths remain **I-D**, **I-ND**, **N-D**, and **N-ND**: income or no income, each with or without debt. Debt means money owed. The income side includes current income or support, not just a job.

The income map has four source groups: employer pay; own work or business; assets; and support or retirement payments. Hourly and salary sit under employer pay. A reader can have several sources.

The debt map groups amounts by how they arose: borrowing or credit; unpaid bills; and taxes, fines, and court-ordered amounts. Cost, purpose, creditor, and payment terms add detail. “Good” and “bad” debt are judgments to examine, not extra starting paths.

These are teaching maps for the workbook. The [research record](/docs/research) documents their evidence and boundaries. [Reader paths](/docs/reader-paths) records how to tag later chapters.

## Where the smaller questions go [#where-the-smaller-questions-go]

| Question or topic                                                                                  | Chapter / section                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Mindset, different priorities, and the dream-day exercise                                          | 2 · The life you want                             |
| Hourly work, salary, business, mixed sources, and salary conversations                             | 3 · Find and grow your income                     |
| Saving from a pay cheque, giving to church, budgets, budgeting apps, banks, and fintech services   | 4 · When you get paid                             |
| Good/bad debt, loans vs lines of credit, tax bills, collections, and debt collectors               | 5 · Make a plan for debt                          |
| Borrowing from or lending to friends and family                                                    | 5 · Make a plan for debt                          |
| Minimum payments, card interest, and debit vs credit                                               | 6 · Credit cards 101                              |
| Credit-score history and when scores matter                                                        | 7 · Credit scores 101                             |
| Expensive purchases and BNPL                                                                       | 8 · Before you buy                                |
| Job loss, moving, marriage, large unplanned costs, and life insurance                              | 9 · When life changes; income recovery links to 3 |
| Get-rich-quick schemes                                                                             | 10 · The promise of fast money                    |
| Investment timing, goals, risk, fees, and access to money                                          | 11 · Before you invest                            |
| Stocks, funds, bonds, Treasuries, real estate, crypto, businesses, private equity, and hedge funds | 12 · Ways to invest                               |

Keep new questions in this map even before their prose is drafted. Add a section within its chapter first. Give it a separate chapter only if its scope calls for one.

## Writing and example rules [#writing-and-example-rules]

* Use generic **$** amounts in worked examples. Keep real source figures intact; any published use needs the correct context.
* Debt includes all money the reader owes. Do not omit an amount because someone calls it good debt.
* Explain each broad group with concrete examples. Keep pay method separate from income source.
* Preserve the author's voice, stories, and respect for different goals.
* Each chapter needs an explanation, an example, steps, and an exercise. Research factual claims before treating a draft as finished.

Sources: [Notes 1–3](/docs/raw-thoughts), [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan), and [Plan decisions](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions).


# Print preview (/docs/print-preview)



This is a first interior design proof using an earlier Chapter 1 draft and its four workbook pages. The online chapter has since received a voice revision; the PDFs and preview images have not yet been regenerated. The book title is still open. Chapters 2–8 and workbook pages 5–18 are available as draft text; they are not included in these PDFs.

## The two sizes [#the-two-sizes]

The **book is 6 × 9 inches**. The **companion workbook is 8½ × 11 inches**, with more room to write. The image below shows them at the same scale.

<img src="/moneybook-planning-pages/print/size-comparison.png" alt="Book and workbook pages shown at the same scale: a 6 by 9 inch reading page beside a larger 8.5 by 11 inch worksheet." width="1587" height="1233" />

Six by nine inches is a common US paperback size. There isn't one required size for a book. This is a starting choice we can change after reviewing the pages. [KDP trim-size guide](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/GVBQ3CMEQW3W2VL6).

The PDF contains the full chapter, including its examples, tables, exercise instructions, and source notes. It uses a serif reading font, clear headings, page numbers, and extra space at the binding edge.

The PDF has four physical pages, matching the references in Chapter 1. Each has blank tables or ruled answer spaces. Dates, interest, fees, and other unknown details remain optional where the chapter says they can wait.

## Try it on paper [#try-it-on-paper]

Print the PDFs at **100% / actual size**. The book PDF is already 6 × 9 inches; on a larger sheet, trim it to that size to judge how it feels. The workbook uses letter-size paper.

These are layout proofs. Page references, margins, and pagination will be checked again when the whole book and the printer are chosen.

The editable wording stays in [Chapter 1](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) and the [companion workbook](/docs/workbook). The PDFs capture the earlier draft. Update the layouts after wording changes, then regenerate the PDFs.


# General plan (/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan)



These are the supplied planning notes, lightly cleaned for spelling and formatting. Open blanks and conflicting labels are retained. The [book plan](/docs/outline) develops them using the recordings.

## The book [#the-book]

This book is not meant to be read front to back. It's a workbook that gives you a practical step-by-step guide on how to \_\_\_\_\_.

Notes:

* Extremely practical guide.
* Backed with facts.
* Stories / examples.

## We will teach people about [#we-will-teach-people-about]

* What should you do when you get paid? How to split up a pay cheque.
* Why get-rich-quick schemes do not work.
* Everyone's financial journey is different and people have different priorities.
* Not everyone is meant to be a business owner or a full-time employee.
* Credit Card 101: interest, minimum payments, and why credit cards are a double-edged sword.
* Debt 101: how to get out of debt, not get into debt, control and manage debt, and balance payments.
* Increasing your monthly income is the number-one priority.
* How to make a decision if you want to buy something expensive.
* Why budgeting apps don't really help you.
* Your mentality about money truly does matter.
* Should you use BNPL apps?
* Investing 101: stocks, real estate, crypto, and investing in businesses.
* Credit Score 101: what it is, when it was created, and whether / when it matters.
* An exercise to figure out how much money you need for your dream lifestyle. Sit down and calculate exactly how much you need.

Each group will have an ID. Each topic will have bullet points or key material meant for the different groups.

## Places where you can start [#places-where-you-can-start]

### Hourly / no full-time job [#hourly--no-full-time-job]

Original heading: “If you don't have a full-time job start here (Debt free version vs No Debt Version).”

Phrasing: “If your monthly income comes from a job that pays you hourly then start here.”

Qualifications listed: you don't have a job, or you get paid hourly.

Paths: if you have any debt, start here; if you don't have debt, start here.

Proposed ID: triangle / Hourly.

### Salary [#salary]

The original heading again says, “If you don't have a full-time job start here.”

Phrasing: “If your monthly income comes from a job that pays you a salary then start here.”

Qualification: you earn a salary.

Paths: if you have debt, start here; if you don't have any debt, start here.

Proposed ID: square / FT folks.

### Business [#business]

Heading: “If you run a business then start here.”

Phrasing: “If ALL your monthly income comes from a business that you are running then start here.”

Qualifications and paths were left blank.

Proposed ID: square / Biz Folks.

## Writing style [#writing-style]

The supplied style direction names a third-grade reading target and fifth-grade maximum, drawing on Alex Hormozi's writing guidelines.

* Use present voice and simple tenses.
* Write in active voice.
* Delete adverbs and use strong, specific verbs.
* Keep sentences short. Aim for a maximum of one comma.
* Choose basic, everyday words.

Supplied references: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/H-MXJIUkSi8), [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@ahormozi/video/7242370736713764139), and [Skool](https://www.skool.com/acquisitionuniversity/alex-hormozis-writing-guidelines-prompt-gpt).

The author also asks for the writing to match the way he speaks in the raw recordings.

# Plan decisions (/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions)



Written follow-up from the author on September 27, 2026. This page preserves the direction behind the revised [book plan](/docs/outline). It is a written note, not an audio transcript.

## Dollars [#dollars]

> just say a generic dollar amount

Use generic $ amounts in examples. This does not select a country's tax or credit rules.

## Debt [#debt]

> debt is money that you are owing

## Income and debt maps [#income-and-debt-maps]

> Okay, so when this where basically what we want to do is that we want to essentially give people— part of this is going to be giving people a definite and a concrete list of examples for each thing. So when we say income, there is actually, like, a finite amount of different types of income. You either earn hourly, you earn a salary, or you earn dividends. I guess if there's any more, you can also add that as well. Same thing with debt. When we say debt, does that mean good debt? Bad debt? What is good debt? What is bad debt? What are the different types of— what are the actual possible different types of debt you can have, like a finite amounts? Not credit card or line of credit. It means, like, you can have debt from borrowing from a friend. You can have— no, I don't even know. I don't know what the best way to go about that is. And then for the income stuff, you can, like, there's streamers, there's social media, but it still all falls under some generic category. So the goal here is I want to be able to give people some sort of accurate, like— how do I put it— accurate mind map of exactly here, the different options that people have. It's one of these things. The same way in Alex Hormozi's books, he's like, there's only four ways for you to earn customers. It's this, this, this, or this. Everything else, everything falls into these four buckets. That's the kind of goal that we're trying to achieve here.

Editorial implementation: group income by its source, then show pay methods and concrete examples underneath. Group debts by how the money became owed, then record the terms. These are teaching maps developed for this workbook.

Further direction from the author for Chapter 1:

> I think for chapter one, you need to explain why the person has to have to see exactly what the total picture is. It's not to scare them. It's literally just because you can't make a plan if you're not able to see it. You need to actually see it, see it, like look at it. Like you have an amount, how much you owe, look at it. And then let's also to where it also asks them to write exactly how much they have, which I. Just write it on paper so you can actually see it, tangibly see it and get comfortable, like thinking about that number. And then there's also funds in which, like show them a paper, like checking your bank account or something like that, if there's any something we should.

Editorial implementation: explain why the reader needs visible numbers to plan. Have them check their accounts and records, write what they have and owe, and put the totals beside income on a sheet of paper. Include a worked example of the sheet. Preserve the difference between today's balances and money received over a month.

## Write what you know for now [#write-what-you-know-for-now]

Further direction from the author for Chapter 1:

> For chapter one, it's kind of crazy that we're asking people already about interest fees and stuff because we don't. I guess it's not that bad because we can just ask them to not feel worried about if they know it or not. If you know it, write it down. If you don't know it, then it's okay. And if you don't know the next payment, then it's okay. We're gonna review all these things later. It's just to get a full idea of where you're at right now.

Editorial implementation: keep payment dates, interest, fees, and terms in the worksheet but make them optional at this stage. Ask readers to write what they know and leave unknown details blank or mark them “not sure yet.” Point to the later chapters that explain those details. A missing amount stays visible as a gap rather than being treated as zero. Chapter 1 gives the reader a picture of their current position without requiring every answer first.

## One next chapter for each path [#one-next-chapter-for-each-path]

Further direction from the author for Chapter 1:

> Um, we can just get them to pick one here. We don't need to make a plan for both. It's just gonna get people confused. So if you have income and debt, you need to, first of all, I think— actually, I don't know what's the best thing to do here. I think that— gosh, I'm so tired. Okay, so I think that if you have income and debt, then let's go to what to do when you get paid first before we go to make a plan for your debt. Then in the income and no debt, you can go to the life you want. You can go to the life you want. And then for the no income and debt, let's just get them to find a job first, because, like, that's the most important thing, to make a plan for the debt yet. And then for the no income or no debt, we can still just go to the income. Let's go to also find and grow your income as well. That way it gives people a more direct guide on what to go for, on what to go into, on what the next steps are, and then, yeah.

Editorial implementation: give each path one next chapter. I-D goes to When you get paid. I-ND goes to The life you want. Both N-D and N-ND go to Find and grow your income. Remove competing next-chapter suggestions from Chapter 1 and use the same routes in the reader-path guide.

## The book and a companion workbook [#the-book-and-a-companion-workbook]

Further direction from the author:

> I think that we need to, for the stuff to fill in, I think that we can also implement some sort of companion workbook as well. So it's two things. It's the book and then the companion workbook, and we can tell people go to this page in the workbook and fill it out there. And if they didn't get the companion workbook, that they can just, like, write it out as well. I feel like that makes sense.

Editorial implementation: keep the book and companion workbook as distinct parts. The book teaches and guides the exercise. The companion holds numbered fill-in pages. Each exercise points to its workbook page and gives plain-paper instructions so the companion stays optional. Start with four pages for Chapter 1. Final printed page references will be set during layout.


# Reader paths (/docs/reader-paths)



The four paths follow [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3). [Chapter 1](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) explains them in the author's voice and guides the first exercise. Readers can use the [companion workbook](/docs/workbook) or plain paper.

## The four starting points [#the-four-starting-points]

| ID   | Starting situation                                       | Next chapter after Chapter 1                                 |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| I-D  | Current income or support, with money owed.              | [When you get paid](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid)        |
| I-ND | Current income or support, with no money owed.           | [The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want)        |
| N-D  | No current income or support source, with money owed.    | [Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income) |
| N-ND | No current income or support source, with no money owed. | [Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income) |

Give each path one next chapter. For I-D, start with incoming money before building a debt plan. Both no-income paths start with finding income. This follows the author's [direction on next steps](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions#one-next-chapter-for-each-path).

These describe a starting point. They do not measure a person's worth, savings, or whether income covers expenses. A path can change.

An ongoing source can pay at uneven times. Someone living from savings alone belongs in a no-income path for this workbook, with those savings recorded beside the path. Keep one-time receipts visible without treating them as ongoing income.

## What counts as debt [#what-counts-as-debt]

The author has defined it: **money you owe**. Include amounts owed to people, lenders, providers, and government. A mortgage and money borrowed from a friend both count. A balance does not stop being debt because it is called “good.”

Include balances already owed even when the payment is not late. Mark due dates so routine bills and overdue amounts are distinguishable. Exclude future purchases that have not happened. Record disputed or uncertain obligations separately for checking.

The goal of income without debt remains part of the author's direction. A definition alone does not settle the order or speed of repayment; those steps belong in [Chapter 5](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt).

## Income-source labels [#income-source-labels]

Use descriptive labels instead of forcing every reader into hourly, salary, or business.

| Label                | Examples on the workbook map                                                       |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Employer             | Hourly pay, salary, tips, commissions, bonuses from employment                     |
| Own work             | Freelance work, a service, products, a business or creator channel the reader runs |
| Assets               | Interest, dividends, rent, royalties                                               |
| Support / retirement | Pensions, cash benefits, regular family support, child support                     |

Hourly and salary are pay methods within Employer. Readers can use multiple labels. A later passage could say **I-D · Employer + Own work**. Use **I-D** alone when the source does not change the step. Use **All readers** for shared material.

Sort each payment once. Keep timing, reliability, business costs, and tax still to cover beside it. Borrowing, savings withdrawals, sales, and one-time gifts have a separate cash-receipts line in Chapter 1.

## Debt details [#debt-details]

The chapter's three groups describe how the amount arose: borrowing or credit, unpaid bills, or taxes, fines, and court-ordered amounts. Then record who is owed, the balance, payment dates, interest and fees, any property pledged, and the purpose.

“Secured,” “unsecured,” “instalment,” and “revolving” describe terms to explain in Chapter 5. “Good” and “bad” describe a judgment to examine. Neither replaces the simple debt yes/no question.

## Symbols [#symbols]

The original triangle and square ideas remain available. Text labels keep the paths clear while the visual symbols are undecided.

Sources: [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3), [Plan decisions](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions), and the [income and debt research](/docs/research).


# Research notes (/docs/research)



Keep the author's experience and point of view visible. Check the claims that go beyond that experience. A chapter placeholder is not finished guidance.

## Decisions made [#decisions-made]

The author answered these in [Plan decisions](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions):

* **Dollar amounts:** use generic $ amounts in examples. There is no need to choose between USD and CAD for a made-up calculation. Real source amounts keep their context.
* **Debt:** money the reader owes. This includes amounts people might call good debt.
* **Income and debt categories:** give a compact map, concrete examples, and a way to handle several sources. Do not use an occupation as an income type.
* **Extra topics:** log each question and place it within a chapter as a section. It does not need a page of its own.
* **Promise and title:** leave them open.

The [book plan](/docs/outline) assigns all current topics to 12 chapters. [Chapter 1](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are) is the first full draft.

## Income map [#income-map]

Checked September 27, 2026. The four groups are an editorial teaching map: Employer, Own work, Assets, and Support / retirement. They regroup common sources found in the official references below; no source establishes exactly these four as a universal taxonomy.

| Source                                                                                                                       | What it supports                                                                                                                                           | Scope                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [BLS Consumer Expenditure glossary](https://www.bls.gov/cex/csxgloss.htm), “Income”                                          | Separates employment, net self-employment, property receipts, retirement, benefits, and regular support. Net business income accounts for operating costs. | US statistical definitions. The workbook regroups them; it does not use this as a tax guide.                      |
| [Census overview of income sources](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/04/income-sources.html), April 2, 2025       | Shows earnings, asset income, social insurance, government transfers, and other income. Supports looking beyond a job title.                               | Five groups in that research tool, not the workbook's four. No population statistics are copied into the chapter. |
| [IRS income overview](https://www.irs.gov/filing/taxable-income)                                                             | Includes royalties, freelance work, and other receipts; its groupings differ from this workbook.                                                           | Used to check coverage only. US tax treatment is not applied to all readers.                                      |
| [CFPB financial glossary](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/youth-financial-education/glossary/) | Definitions of dividends and take-home pay.                                                                                                                | General concepts from a US consumer-education source.                                                             |
| [Investor.gov: Capital gain](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/capital-gain)         | A realized gain concerns profit on a sale, not the whole cash receipt.                                                                                     | The $800 / $1,000 example is invented arithmetic, excludes fees and tax, and promises no return.                  |

### Boundaries used in the draft [#boundaries-used-in-the-draft]

Income source, payment method, and timing answer different questions. Hourly and salary describe pay methods. A streamer may receive several kinds of payment. Chapter 1 sorts the payment and counts it once.

Borrowed money and transfers from the reader's own savings are not new earnings. One-time gifts and sale receipts are tracked separately so they are not assumed to repeat. Gain on a sale stays with that sale record to avoid double counting. A business's sales and its payment to its owner must not both be counted as separate personal income.

The cash worksheet records costs or tax still to cover. Noncash support is noted separately. The source groups are for planning; tax definitions and reporting rules need the relevant country when those subjects are drafted.

## Debt map [#debt-map]

Checked September 27, 2026. The author defines debt as money owed. The draft sorts it by how the amount arose: borrowing or credit; unpaid bills; and taxes, fines, and court-ordered amounts. Creditor, purpose, security, and repayment terms remain separate details.

| Source                                                                                                                                                                     | What it supports                                                                                                                   | Scope                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [CFPB financial glossary](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/youth-financial-education/glossary/)                                               | Debt is money owed; collateral, loans, and secured/unsecured lending describe distinct features.                                   | Definitions only. No universal collection procedure or legal outcome is asserted.                               |
| [CFPB debt worksheet](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/documents/5288/cfpb_ymyg_disabilities_debt-worksheet.pdf), pages 1–2                                                 | Includes friends/family, bills, taxes, fines, loans, and support obligations. Records creditor, balance, payment, rate, and terms. | Supports coverage of the inventory. The three-group arrangement and the book's worksheet are editorial choices. |
| [CFPB Consumer voices on financial rules to live by](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201603_cfpb_rules-to-live-by_consumer-voices-report.pdf), March 2016, section 3.3 | Participants disagreed on which debts were good or bad.                                                                            | Qualitative focus groups. This is not proof that a particular debt is safe or harmful.                          |

The workbook includes amounts already owed even if not overdue. It separates future spending plans, disputed amounts, and business obligations that may not be the reader's own. Repayment priority still needs researched guidance and concrete examples.

## Checking the balances [#checking-the-balances]

The author asked readers to see their numbers on paper so they have a starting point for a plan. Chapter 1 now includes current money, income for a stated month, and total money owed. A made-up sheet shows the three totals without adding balances and income together. Other assets stay on a separate list with dates and estimates marked.

Checked September 27, 2026: [CFPB's overdraft guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/bank-accounts/know-your-overdraft-options/), updated June 4, 2025, explains that transactions may not update balances at once. The worksheet therefore records the displayed balance labels, dates, and pending items. The [CFPB glossary](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/youth-financial-education/glossary/) supports the distinction between owned funds and credit limits or overdrafts. No US-specific fees or account rights are generalized to every reader.

The sheet is a record of balances, not a calculation of spendable money or net worth. It uses one current balance per account, keeps available figures as notes, and records negative account balances as debts once. An old statement stays marked for checking; incomplete current totals are labelled partial. Income and support have their own subtotal, separate from other cash receipts. The reason for writing and looking at the figures comes from the author's [follow-up direction](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions#seeing-the-full-picture-on-paper); no psychological outcome is claimed.

## Chapter 2: Costing a chosen life [#chapter-2-costing-a-chosen-life]

Checked October 1, 2026 for the first draft of [Chapter 2](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want), its [spoken adaptation](/docs/scripts/the-life-you-want), and workbook pages 5–7. The desired-life exercise and voice come from Notes 3–4. The household worksheet is an editorial arrangement, not a method claimed to be prescribed by an agency.

No mortgage rules or behavioral statistics are adopted.                                    |

Its result does not establish affordability on each payment date.                              |

Costs or tax still to cover are deducted once or marked unknown.                                   |

### Michelle's rebuilt example [#michelles-rebuilt-example]

All amounts are explicitly fictional generic-dollar assumptions. The chapter retains the source's desired work, family time, and chosen comforts, then settles a customer-service role for the example. It does not assert an actual school, product price, household, or outcome.

* Monthly rows total $8,400: $5,900 costs/payments plus $2,500 saving.
* The assumed partner contribution is $2,400, leaving a $6,000 personal target. Michelle's assumed current take-home pay is $3,000, so the gap is $3,000. Equivalently, $8,400 minus $5,400 current household income is $3,000.
* The $6,000 moving goal less $1,200 assigned savings leaves $4,800. Over 24 months that is $200 per month, already included in $2,500 saving. The remaining $2,300 is for other saving goals, including a cash reserve.
* The car payment appears inside transport only. Other debt payments exclude it. The example assumes no further up-front purchases and no additional costs or tax still to cover in the take-home figures.
* The $200 monthly provision for less frequent costs represents $2,400 per year. Actual due dates remain separate.

The raw $6,500-before-tax/$600 target and $20/$200 weekly cleaning ambiguity are not resolved. The draft avoids treating them as settled facts: it chooses an $800 monthly cleaning allowance without asserting frequency and uses a new, fully labeled household calculation. Local costs, taxes, and future prices need new estimates for a real reader. The script uses the same figures and refers listeners to the full table.

Chapter 3 develops the earning routes and adviser story. It replaces the uncertain sales/app figures with a separate, explicitly fictional editing calculation. Existing Chapter 1 print proofs do not include Chapters 2–8 or workbook pages 5–18; their layout remains future work.

## Chapter 3: Choosing an income step [#chapter-3-choosing-an-income-step]

### Author material and editorial choices [#author-material-and-editorial-choices]

* Note 3 supplies the goal: income serves the chosen life. Chapter 3 does not require every reader with existing income to increase it.
* Notes 5–6 supply the direct push to seek work and consider temporary roles. The student and stay-at-home-parent qualifications stay beside the advice. The chapter adds practical checks for health, access, care costs, and permission to work; these are editorial guidance, not new personal stories.
* Note 4 at 04:11–08:22 supports the Starbucks conversation, vehicle analogy, and founder-versus-product reflection. The chapter retells it without a direct adviser quote, uncertain company name, or claim that a career change has already succeeded.
* Note 4 at 15:02–20:03 supplies the idea of exploring writing/business routes. Audience-growth guarantees, speculative conversions, guessed tax, and inconsistent subscription calculations are excluded. They remain raw source material.
* No claim is made that a temporary job, pay request, business test, or benefits check will produce income. Actual pay, availability, terms, and eligibility require current local information.

### Example and exercise checks [#example-and-exercise-checks]

Michelle remains fictional. Her Chapter 2 household target is $8,400; the partner contribution is $2,400; her personal target is $6,000. Current take-home pay is $3,000, leaving a $3,000 monthly gap. Her editing test uses two hours, no spending, a Friday action deadline, and a Sunday review. It has no assumed earnings.

The separate fictional paid editing batch has four jobs at $150 = $600 received. Assumed total business costs of $120 leave $480 before tax. Eight delivery hours plus four customer-finding/admin hours = 12 hours; $480 / 12 = $40 before tax per recorded hour. All customers are assumed to have paid within the reviewed period. These are not market prices, employee wages, Michelle's results, or a forecast of repeating income. With tax unknown, the $480 cannot be treated as take-home money toward her gap.

Pages 8–9 mirror the chapter's five steps: starting point, limits, options, action, and review. They keep possible income separate from receipts, include payment dates and remaining costs/tax, and work on plain paper. All four reader paths point next to Chapter 4, while no-income readers retain their immediate income/support action and shortfall needs.

### Recording and arithmetic decisions [#recording-and-arithmetic-decisions]

Note 9's correction at 03:02 puts bill planning before choosing a saving percentage. The draft preserves the mother's advice, habit-building aim, conditional 25–30% suggestion, Christian tithing practice, and admission of shortfalls. It excludes unclear speech near 16:29, assumed universal pay frequency, guessed phone-plan prices, and claims about guaranteed returns from giving. No biblical text is quoted or interpreted.

All examples use fictional generic dollars and are separate from Michelle:

* Main month: $5,000 take-home − $2,500 required costs − $1,250 saving = $1,250 left to allocate. Saving is 25% of $5,000. Required costs include later known-bill provisions; no additional tax, business costs, or giving are assumed.
* Small surplus: $2,000 − $1,600 = $400. Saving 25% of $400 = $100, leaving $300. This is 5% of initial take-home, not 25%. The source's changing $500/$300/$400 remainder is not treated as one settled figure.
* Separate giving case: $5,000 − $500 giving − $2,500 required costs − $1,125 saving = $875. Giving is 10% of take-home; saving is 25% of the $4,500 after giving. This completion is editorial, not a quoted source calculation or prescribed split.
* Timing: first $2,500 receipt − $2,000 costs = $500 carried. Add the second $2,500; subtract $500 required costs, $1,250 saving, and $1,250 allocated elsewhere = $0 unassigned. Attempting $625 saving in the first period leaves a $125 gap. The illustration assumes the next month's receipt precedes the next month's costs; readers must check their own dates.
* Shortfall: $1,500 needs/required payments − $1,200 available = $300 uncovered. Saving, giving, optional purchases, expected assistance, and unconfirmed arrangements do not silently close it.

Pages 10–12 record the allocation, date-by-date plan, shortfall consequences and contacts, and payday review. Projected receipts stay distinct from cash available now. Transfers and reservations must not be counted twice. Actual consequences, assistance, due-date changes, fees, tax, and coverage remain dependent on country and provider.

| [CFPB collector checks](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-tell-if-a-debt-collector-is-legitimate-or-a-scam-en-1699/), [validation information](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-information-does-a-debt-collector-have-to-give-me-about-the-debt-en-331/)                                                            | US verification and covered-collector validation process, including the timely written-dispute condition. Not all creditors or other countries are covered.  |
| [CFPB family lending](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/adult-financial-education/tips-for-managing-family-lending-and-borrowing/)                                                                                                                                                                                    | Clarify whether money is a gift or loan, record terms, and discuss changed circumstances. No family-loan tax threshold is asserted.                          |

Note 3 supplies the author's admission of debt after job loss and moving; no recovery is invented. Notes 7 and 9 supply the borrowing and shortfall questions. Uncertain exchange-rate amounts and the unfinished line-of-credit recommendation remain excluded.

Fictional Sam: $3,000 take-home − $2,400 non-debt needs/planned costs − $100 reserve = $500 for debt. Required payments $80 + $220 + $50 = $350, leaving $150 extra. Card payment becomes $230. For one explicitly simplified monthly interest calculation: $2,000 × 24% / 12 = $40; $3,000 × 12% / 12 = $30. Closing balances $1,810 + $2,810 + $350 = $4,970. Total reduction is $430, not the $500 paid. The same first-month total under the alternative allocation does not establish equal lifetime interest. With income $2,700, only $200 remains for $350 required payments: $150 short.

Workbook page 14 starts before bills and debt payments, then subtracts each commitment once. The primary integration review checked the source admission, calculations, worksheets, chapter routes, and the material line-of-credit and validation-notice claims against their primary pages.

Assumptions exclude compounding and changing balances.
