# 8. Before you buy — spoken script (/docs/scripts/before-you-buy)



**Spoken adaptation · First draft.** Based on [Chapter 8](/docs/chapters/before-you-buy). This is developed prose, not a raw transcript.

## The script [#the-script]

You want the thing. The headphones, the camera, the car. Okay. What happens to the rest of your money if you buy it?

I love cars. They make me happy. I don't think you have to pretend a purchase is going to earn money before you're allowed to want it. Your quality of life matters too.

But I don't want you to buy something you wanted and then hate the payments. So let's think about it now.

For an unplanned purchase over two hundred and fifty dollars, I try to have enough to pay for it twice. If the headphones cost three hundred and fifty, I want seven hundred available.

That's my personal rule. I don't get it right every time. Something goes on sale, and suddenly I'm explaining to myself why I need it. So the rule gives me a pause.

I'm talking about an unplanned purchase. If you've been saving for something, check that plan and what the purchase leaves behind. I'm not saying you need to save for the same thing twice. An urgent need is a different decision too. My rule isn't a reason to leave an essential need unmet.

And we need to check what “available” means. If you've got seven hundred in the account and the rent needs seven hundred, you don't have seven hundred for headphones.

Here's an invented example from the chapter. You have eighteen hundred in cash. Eleven hundred is already assigned to bills, debt, tax, saving, giving, and other commitments. That leaves seven hundred free.

Buy the three-hundred-and-fifty-dollar headphones, and you have three hundred and fifty free afterward. The account still has fourteen hundred and fifty in it, but eleven hundred of that still has a job. Don't spend it twice.

You could buy a suitable two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar pair and keep four hundred and fifty free. You could keep what you have and leave all seven hundred alone. Those are choices. Write down which one you're making and why.

Now, let's talk about money that hasn't come in yet.

I've fallen into this doing software work on the side. You have a conversation about a job. You expect a payment. In your mind, you've already started spending it. Then the money doesn't arrive when you expected. The expense is still there.

Let's say you're expecting ten thousand from a job and you spend two thousand on a computer before you're paid. Those numbers illustrate the pattern. The money still has to arrive, while the purchase has already happened.

If the purchase can wait, wait for the payment. Then count the costs, tax, and other commitments it still has to cover. Next week's paycheck isn't money in the account today either.

And don't use a card limit as the answer. A two-thousand-dollar limit doesn't tell you whether a fifteen-hundred-dollar camera fits your own plan. Go back to the money you can use and how you'll pay the bill.

Buy now, pay later needs the same attention. It's borrowing. One small payment might seem fine. Then you get another, and another. They stack up.

Write every payment down. The amount today. The later amounts and dates. The full amount you owe. The terms and any costs. Then put those dates beside the payments you've already agreed to make.

The chapter invents a plan for the three-hundred-and-fifty-dollar headphones: four payments of eighty-seven fifty, two weeks apart, with no interest or fees assumed. It's a maths example, not a product offer.

After the first payment, you still owe two hundred and sixty-two fifty for the headphones. If another sixty-dollar payment and a ninety-dollar payment fall before the next instalment, those three payments need two hundred and thirty-seven fifty altogether. And your other bills are still there.

Check the actual agreement. Fees and automatic-payment arrangements differ. A small instalment doesn't tell you the full cost.

If you're already struggling with required payments, I'd go back to that problem before taking on another loan for something optional.

The same thinking applies to a car. Yes, it can be something you enjoy. But count the whole cost and the whole loan. Insurance, fuel, maintenance, the things you'll have to pay to keep using it. Then look at what would happen in a lower-income month.

Would you still enjoy the car if its payments took away something else you care about?

Okay, now pick one purchase and use workbook page eighteen, or plain paper. Name it and say why you want it. Work out the money available after commitments. Compare the choices and their full costs. Put any payments on the calendar.

Then make a decision: buy, save first, choose something else, wait, or check a missing detail. Give yourself a next action and a date.

You can want the thing. I just want you to see what getting it would mean for the rest of your life.

## Exercise and source notes [#exercise-and-source-notes]

Use [18. My purchase check](/docs/workbook/my-purchase-check) or the plain-paper instructions in [Chapter 8](/docs/chapters/before-you-buy#your-turn). The chapter includes the filled tables, urgent-needs qualification, and separate next chapter for each reader path.

Voice and personal material come from [Note 9, 19:02–end](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-9#1902040). The script preserves the correction to $250 and the saved-for exception. Added cash and instalment examples are fictional and match the chapter. US factual support: [CFPB BNPL explanation](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-buy-now-pay-later-bnpl-loan-en-2119/), [BNPL fees](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/do-buy-now-pay-later-bnpl-loans-have-fees-en-2118/), and [auto-loan comparisons](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-compare-auto-loan-offers-what-should-i-look-at-besides-the-monthly-payment-en-753/), checked October 1, 2026. Product terms and country rules need their own checks.


# 6. Credit cards 101 — spoken script (/docs/scripts/credit-cards)



**Draft spoken adaptation.** Based on [Chapter 6](/docs/chapters/credit-cards) and [Note 7](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-7), especially 01:05–04:25 and 08:04–11:09. This is edited prose, not a transcript. The example is invented and uses generic dollars; the linked financial guidance is US guidance.

## Script [#script]

Have you ever paid with your phone and barely thought about it? You tap, take your stuff, and leave. Then the bill comes.

That's what worries me about credit cards. Spending is easy. Keeping track of what you've borrowed takes more work. And I'm including myself in that. I'm still working on managing debt too.

There can be benefits. You might get points from something you were already going to buy. But are you buying what you need, or are you buying more to get the points?

Let's say a made-up offer pays 2% back. You spend an extra $100 on things you didn't want and earn $2. You still spent $98. That's why I want us to look at the bill before the rewards.

Okay, here's a fictional bill. It closes on April 30 with an $800 statement balance. The minimum is $30, due May 25. Then you make a new $100 purchase on May 3. Nothing else changes. Now the posted balance is $900.

If you pay $30, you haven't cleared the bill. You have $870 left before any later interest or activity. If you pay $800, you've covered the April statement. The later $100 is still owed. Paying $900 covers both amounts in this example.

Those figures come from a made-up card with no earlier carried balance, no fees, and an active purchase grace period. Your card may be different. On US cards, a purchase grace period can depend on paying in full under the card's terms. Carrying a balance can remove it, and cash advances generally start accruing interest right away. Check your own agreement. [CFPB: grace periods](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/).

Now let's turn that bill into a plan. Where will the payment come from? What else does that money need to cover? Which date will you send it? And how will you check that it went through?

For the example, you might have $900 already reserved. You pay the $800 statement in time and keep $100 for the later purchase. You don't spend that $100 again. It already has a job.

If you can't make the minimum, write that down too. Contact the issuer and explain what you can pay. Ask what help is available and what the terms would be. Don't assume help has been agreed just because you've asked. [CFPB: payment difficulty](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_adult-fin-ed_act-fast-pay-credit-cards.pdf).

Use workbook page 15, My card statement, and page 16, My card payment plan. Plain paper works. Write your balances, the rate and fees, the minimum, and the due date. Then write the funded payment and your next check.

The useful result is a bill you understand and a payment you can explain. Start there.

## Exercise and next page [#exercise-and-next-page]

Use [page 15](/docs/workbook/my-card-statement) and [page 16](/docs/workbook/my-card-payment-plan), or the same headings on paper. Readers with income go next to [Chapter 7](/docs/chapters/credit-scores). Readers without income go next to [Chapter 3](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), while following through on any urgent payment contact.


# 7. Credit scores 101 — spoken script (/docs/scripts/credit-scores)



**Draft spoken adaptation.** Based on [Chapter 7](/docs/chapters/credit-scores) and the questions in [Note 7](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-7), around 06:47–07:45 and 09:20–10:33. This is edited prose, not a transcript. The system described is the United States; the worked figures are invented.

## Script [#script]

What is a credit score? And what are you supposed to do with it?

If you're getting ready to borrow for a home, you probably want to know what a lender sees. But if you need money for food this week, checking a number again and again won't fix that. Let's understand what it does.

A US credit report holds information about your credit accounts and payment history. A score uses report information to estimate credit behavior. The report is the record. The score is a calculation based on it. [CFPB: reports](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-report-en-309/), [scores](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-credit-score-en-315/).

So start by reading the record. Do you know these accounts? Are the balances and payments right? If something looks wrong, compare the dates and your own statements before deciding it's an error.

Here's an example. One card reports $600 owed with a $2,000 limit. That's 30% of the limit. Another card reports zero owed with a $3,000 limit. Together, that's $600 out of $5,000, or 12%.

That calculation is called credit utilization. It describes how much available credit is being used. It doesn't tell us whether you can afford the $600. It also doesn't give you permission to spend until you reach some percentage. [FICO: amounts owed](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-scores/amount-of-debt).

And you don't need to carry a card balance and pay interest just to build a good score. Keep the payment plan in view. [CFPB: building credit](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-and-keep-a-good-credit-score-en-318/).

Say you open a report and find a paid account still showing $400. That's our invented example. Check the report's date against your payoff receipt. If it still appears wrong, use the provider's inquiry or dispute process with the records that support you. In the US, the CFPB explains how to contact both the bureau and the business that supplied the information. [CFPB: disputes](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-an-error-on-my-credit-report-en-314/).

Now you've got an action: check this account, send the record if needed, and follow up. That's something you can do. “Get a perfect score” doesn't tell you what to do today.

Use workbook page 17, My credit check. You can use paper instead. Write why you're checking, where the report came from, its date, and what you need to check. If you have a score, record which model it is and when it was calculated. If you don't, keep going with the report.

Then pick one action and a date. If the record is accurate but you can't cover a payment, the action belongs in your debt and income plan. If it's wrong, work on the error. You don't have to solve every money problem by moving one number.

## Exercise and next page [#exercise-and-next-page]

Use [page 17](/docs/workbook/my-credit-check) and [Chapter 7's country-specific access steps](/docs/chapters/credit-scores#read-it-then-act-on-what-you-find). Readers with income go next to [Chapter 8](/docs/chapters/before-you-buy). Readers without income go next to [Chapter 3](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income), while following up on urgent debt or report issues.


# 3. Find and grow your income — spoken script (/docs/scripts/grow-your-income)



**Spoken adaptation · First draft.** Based on [Chapter 3](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income). This is developed prose, not a transcript of a recording.

## The script [#the-script]

What could bring money in from where you are today?

If you have no income, need money coming in, and can work, I think you need to widen the search. Apply for work you can do. Don't leave a job out just because it isn't at the company you had in mind.

It can be temporary. You can still work toward something else.

Now, that has to fit your actual life. Being a stay-at-home parent is a responsibility. Studying takes time. Health, care duties, transport, and permission to work can limit your options. So start with what you can do. If you need support, make checking that part of the plan. If essentials aren't covered today, a possible job next month doesn't close that gap today.

But if the only thing stopping you from applying is that the job doesn't look like the one you imagined, I'd ask you to look again.

I had a conversation with someone at Starbucks about choosing how to get to a goal. Think about trying to get to the top of a sand dune in a Ferrari. You've decided on the car. But does it suit where you're trying to go?

For me, I had this idea of being a tech founder. Then I thought about what I wanted from that. I wanted a say in how a product works, how it's designed, and how it's built. That helped me look at the goal differently.

So what do you want from your work?

If your job gives you the money and the time you need, you don't have to start a business. If it doesn't, we can look at what might change. The hours. The pay. The role. Or something you do yourself.

Let's go back to Michelle. She's our fictional example. Her household plan costs eight thousand four hundred dollars a month. Her partner covers two thousand four hundred. That leaves six thousand for her. Her take-home pay is three thousand, so there's a three-thousand-dollar gap.

She wants more time for writing and research. She also wants to be there for school pickup. So we're looking at money and time together.

She could look at a writing job. She could test an editing service. She could work on a book. Those are options to check. None of them is money coming in yet.

For this example, she keeps her job and starts with one small check. Two hours this week. No spending. She makes a sample with text she owns and asks three possible customers about their needs by Friday. On Sunday, she reviews what she learned.

That's the step. She hasn't closed the gap. She's finding out whether this is worth more time.

And when money does come in, count it properly. In the chapter, we invent a batch of four editing jobs at a hundred and fifty dollars each. That's six hundred received. We assume a hundred and twenty in business costs, leaving four hundred and eighty before tax. We count the unpaid admin and customer-finding time too.

That isn't take-home pay. It isn't a promise of more jobs next week. It's a way to look at what one batch actually gave you.

Okay, now do this for yourself. Use workbook pages eight and nine, or plain paper. Write down your starting point and what limits your options. Compare two possible routes if you have two. What do you know, and what do you need to check?

Then pick one action. Give it a date and a limit on the time and money you'll use. Pick a day to look at what happened.

If your first step is a support application, write that. If it's a job application, write that. If it's a conversation about pay, write that.

You don't need to figure out your whole career today. You do need to know what you're going to do next.

## Exercise and source notes [#exercise-and-source-notes]

Use [8. My income options](/docs/workbook/my-income-options) and [9. My next income step](/docs/workbook/my-next-income-step). The full [Chapter 3 exercise](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income#your-turn) works on plain paper and covers costs, tax, uncertainty, and payment dates.

Voice and ideas: [Notes 5–6](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-5) for the opening; [Note 4, 04:11–08:22](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-4#0411840) for the adviser retelling; Note 4's Michelle and income-route discussion for the fictional example. The spoken adaptation uses the same settled assumptions as Chapters 2–3. It adds no claim that Michelle has earned from editing. See [Chapter 3 research](/docs/research#chapter-3-choosing-an-income-step) for the supporting checks.

# 5. Make a plan for debt — spoken script (/docs/scripts/make-a-plan-for-debt)



**Draft adaptation of [Chapter 5](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt).** This is a speaking script, not a transcript. The chapter holds full product explanations and country-specific sources.

## Script [#script]

What do you do when you owe money and every dollar coming in already has somewhere to go?

I've been there. I lost my job during my honeymoon. My wife and I moved to New York with wedding debt, and I spent a lot of time living on credit. When I recorded these thoughts, I was still trying to work my way out of that hole.

So let's start with what you actually owe. The card. The loan. The unpaid bill. The money your friend lent you. Even the thing someone told you was good debt. If you owe it, put it on the page.

Now add the details. Who gets paid? How much is due? When? What rate and fees apply? Is anything already overdue? Is there a car or home pledged as backup?

A credit limit isn't your income. An overdraft isn't extra pay. If the money came from borrowing, you still need a way to pay it back. Check your agreement rather than guessing from the name on the product.

Before choosing which balance to pay down faster, deal with right now. What needs paying so you can eat, stay housed, and keep working? Are there notices or deadlines you need help with? Put those on the page.

Sometimes there's a shortfall. I know. If there isn't enough, don't write a repayment plan using money you don't have. Find the gap. Check what can change. Contact the people you owe and find out what options they actually offer. Write down anything they agree to.

Okay, let's say the required payments fit and you have something extra. You could aim it at the highest rate. Or aim it at the smallest balance to get that one finished. Keep the other agreed payments in the plan.

Here's a made-up example. Sam brings home $3,000 this month. His non-debt needs and planned costs take $2,400. He keeps $100 for unexpected needs. That leaves $500 for his debts.

His card requires $80. His personal loan requires $220. He agreed to pay his sister $50. That's $350 required, leaving $150 extra.

He puts the extra toward his card. So the card gets $230, the loan gets $220, and his sister gets $50. All together, $500.

In the chapter's simplified example, $70 of interest is added before those payments. His total debt starts at $5,400 and ends at $4,970. He paid $500, but the balance went down by $430. The statement matters. Some of the payment covered interest.

Now if his income drops, this plan changes. We can't just keep the same extra payment because it looked good on paper last month.

And if money is owed to someone you know, talk clearly. Is it a gift or a loan? What did you agree? If you need more time, have that conversation. Don't quietly treat their money as the payment that doesn't count.

Use workbook pages 13 and 14, or two sheets of paper. First, your debt details. Then, your plan. Write the amount you can pay, the dates, and the next action. If the next action is a call or finding income, write that. It still counts as work you need to do.

Then choose a date to look again. What got paid? What was added? What do you owe now?

You don't have to solve every balance today. But you do need to know what happens next.

## Source and recording notes [#source-and-recording-notes]

Personal experience: [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3). Borrowing distinctions: [Note 7](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-7). Shortfall voice and conditions: [Note 9, 14:01–18:42](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-9). The borrowing point is supported by [FCAC's line-of-credit explanation](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/loans-lines-credit.html) and [overdraft explanation](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/banking/overdraft-protection.html). Repayment approaches: [CFPB comparison](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-reduce-your-debt/). Family agreements: [CFPB guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/adult-financial-education/tips-for-managing-family-lending-and-borrowing/).

Sam is fictional. His figures match the chapter's stated assumptions. For tax notices or collections, use the chapter's scoped guidance rather than treating this shorter script as a legal process.


# Chapter 2: The life you want (/docs/scripts/the-life-you-want)



*Spoken draft adapted from [Chapter 2](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want). Read with the chapter's worked table and workbook pages 5–7 available. This is edited prose, not a transcript or a recording of the author.*

## Where are you trying to go? [#where-are-you-trying-to-go]

Okay, so you've put your money on paper. You know what you have. You can see what comes in and what you owe.

Now I want you to think about the life you're trying to get to. What does that actually look like?

Let's say you want to get up early, go to the gym, take your kids to school, and be home for dinner. Great. Let's write that down. Maybe you don't want kids. Maybe you want to travel. Maybe your priority is knowing the bills are covered. Write your own version.

I want you to get into the details. Where do you live? What do you spend your day doing? What do you want time for?

Take a minute and put that on workbook page 5, My chosen life. Or write it on paper. Then mark what matters most and what you could change.

## Put numbers beside it [#put-numbers-beside-it]

Now let's look at Michelle. She's the fictional person in this chapter. She wants to spend her working day thinking, researching, and writing. Being available for her kids matters to her. She also wants a nicer car, cleaning help, and money going into savings.

We've made up a complete set of amounts to show the calculation. These aren't quotes for what your life will cost.

Her household plan comes to $8,400 a month. That includes $2,500 in saving. It also includes the bills, the car costs, care, and payments on existing debt.

There's a moving goal too. It costs $6,000 in this example. She already has $1,200 set aside, so she needs another $4,800. Over 24 months, that's $200 a month. That $200 is already inside her saving total. Count it once.

For this example, her partner contributes $2,400 a month. So Michelle needs to bring in $6,000. We're talking about money after deductions and any costs or tax still to cover.

Right now, we're giving her $3,000 a month in take-home pay. So there's a $3,000 gap.

But remember what she wanted her day to look like. If a job gives her the money but means she can never do the school pickup, she still has something to work through.

## Your numbers [#your-numbers]

Use workbook page 6, What that life costs. Or write a list with the cost, how often you pay it, its monthly share, and where the number came from. Keep one-time goals separate, then include their monthly saving amount once.

You don't know a number yet? Write that down too. We can come back to it.

Then use page 7, My target and next step. Compare your target with income for the same person or household, after costs and tax still to cover. Keep the period the same. If your income changes, show the range. Keep gaps in the information visible.

The full example and the steps are in the chapter. Pause here if you want to work through them.

## Choose a next step [#choose-a-next-step]

Pick one thing to check or explore. Give it a date. You don't have to solve your whole life on this page.

If you have income and debt, go to Chapter 4, When you get paid. For the other three paths, go to Chapter 3, Find and grow your income. If you have no income or support, finding income comes first; you can come back to the future estimates.

Keep the life you described beside your current money picture. Now you have a starting point and somewhere you want to go.

## Source and delivery notes [#source-and-delivery-notes]

The voice and goal exercise come from [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) and [Note 4](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-4), chiefly 01:00–04:25 and 08:45–15:23. Michelle's figures are the rebuilt fictional example in [Chapter 2](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want#lets-walk-through-michelles-plan), not claims about the author's income or current market prices. The chapter links the primary sources for the planning method and defines the example's limits.

Keep the pauses natural. Show the chapter's full table when reading the numbers; do not present this short script as the entire costing exercise.


# 4. When you get paid — spoken script (/docs/scripts/when-you-get-paid)



**Spoken adaptation · First draft.** Based on [Chapter 4](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid). This is developed prose, not a raw transcript.

## The script [#the-script]

Okay, so you've been paid. What happens next?

My mom used to tell me to pay myself first. And I think there's value in that. You want to get into the habit of putting something away, instead of spending everything and hoping there's money left at the end.

But before we choose a percentage, we need to look at your bills.

What does this money have to cover? Rent? Food? Getting to work? Debt payments? When does each one need to be paid?

Write it down. Look through the whole month and check for bigger bills coming later. Don't spend on a subscription just because its payment comes out before rent. That rent money is already needed, even while you can see it sitting in your account.

Let's use an example. This is a fictional plan with generic dollars. Five thousand comes in after tax. We're assuming no more business costs or tax to take out. All the required costs and payments, including money needed for later known bills, come to two thousand five hundred.

If you can afford to save twenty-five percent of the full five thousand, that's one thousand two hundred and fifty. You have one thousand two hundred and fifty left to allocate after those costs and saving.

That can go toward chosen spending, extra debt payments, or more money kept aside. It doesn't mean you have to use it all.

And if you can't save that amount, don't force the number.

Here's a smaller example. Two thousand comes in after tax. Required costs are sixteen hundred. There's four hundred left. If you choose to save a quarter of that four hundred, you save a hundred and have three hundred left to allocate.

A quarter of the remainder. That's a different amount from a quarter of your whole pay. Write down which one you mean.

Now, giving. I'm a Christian, and tithing is part of how I handle my money. What has helped me is to treat that ten percent as already set aside and plan with the rest. That's my faith and my practice.

From five thousand take-home, that's five hundred for giving and forty-five hundred to plan with. In this separate example, say the required costs are still twenty-five hundred. If you save twenty-five percent of the forty-five hundred after giving, that's eleven hundred and twenty-five. You have eight hundred and seventy-five left to allocate.

The chapter has the full table. The point is to do the math again. You can't add giving to the old plan and leave every other amount where it was. And a percentage doesn't fix a shortage.

The dates matter too. If your money comes in twice a month but most of your bills come out after the first payment, splitting everything exactly in half may leave you short. Put the receipts and bills on a calendar. Keep a running balance. Future money stays marked as expected until it arrives.

If the dates don't fit, ask the provider about your options. A request isn't a confirmed change. Find out what you still need to pay and when.

Now, what if there just isn't enough?

I'm not going to pretend I've always been able to cover everything. Sometimes you can't.

Write down the gap. If you have twelve hundred available and fifteen hundred in needs and required payments, you're three hundred short. There's no new saving or optional spending in that example. We can't make the gap disappear by putting it in a different column.

Look at what could happen if each bill is late. What protects your basic needs, housing, and ability to earn? Who do you need to contact? What help can you check? Use the actual dates and consequences in your situation. My priority list won't be exactly the same as yours.

Record any arrangement that's confirmed. Keep the unpaid amount visible. If nothing has changed, the gap is still there.

Use workbook pages ten to twelve, or plain paper. Make the payment plan. Put it on a calendar. Use the shortfall page if you need it.

And when payday comes, check what actually arrived. Then use the plan. Change it when the facts change.

## Exercise and source notes [#exercise-and-source-notes]

The [full chapter exercise](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid#your-turn) covers current versus expected money, costs and tax, date checks, transfers, and all four reader paths. Workbook pages: [10. My next payment plan](/docs/workbook/my-next-payment-plan), [11. My bill calendar](/docs/workbook/my-bill-calendar), [12. When money falls short](/docs/workbook/when-money-falls-short).

Voice and personal passages come from [Note 9, 00:00–18:42](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-9). The shortfall and completed calculations use the same labeled assumptions as Chapter 4. Giving is presented as the author's practice without a financial-return promise. [Chapter 4 research](/docs/research#chapter-4-planning-a-payday) records the supporting sources.


# Buying something expensive (/docs/topics/big-purchases)



**Chapter destination:** [8. Before you buy](/docs/chapters/before-you-buy). The destination chapter now has a first draft and a spoken adaptation. These remain supporting source notes; the chapter holds the developed exercise and scoped research.

## The reader's question [#the-readers-question]

How do I decide whether to buy something expensive?

The book should give the reader a process they can repeat. It needs to connect the purchase to what they want from life, what it costs, and their current income and debt.

## Exercise to build [#exercise-to-build]

Ask the reader to name the purchase and explain what it adds to their life. Then build a worked comparison of the available choices and their full costs. The final result should be a decision with reasons.

Use the [life you want exercise](/docs/topics/dream-lifestyle) for context. Put financing details in [Debt 101](/docs/topics/debt) and [Buy now, pay later](/docs/topics/bnpl).

Sources: [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) and [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan).


# Buy now, pay later (/docs/topics/bnpl)

# Credit cards 101 (/docs/topics/credit-cards)

The plan calls credit cards a double-edged sword. The chapter needs to explain the useful parts and the risks with a worked example.

## What to cover [#what-to-cover]

* Interest and the meaning of an annual interest rate.
* Minimum payments and what they do to the balance.
* The difference between using credit and carrying debt.

# Debt 101 (/docs/topics/debt)



**Chapter destination:** [5. Make a plan for debt](/docs/chapters/make-a-plan-for-debt). The destination chapter now has a first draft and a spoken adaptation. These remain supporting source notes; the chapter holds the developed exercise and scoped research.

## What to cover [#what-to-cover]

The written plan asks how to get out of debt, avoid new debt, control debt, and balance payments.

[Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) adds questions about collections, debt collectors, tax bills, loans, and lines of credit. These are planned sections of Chapter 5, alongside borrowing from and lending to friends.

## Build around the starting situation [#build-around-the-starting-situation]

I-D and N-D need distinct guidance. In the recording, the author puts finding income first for someone who has none. That idea needs a researched sequence which also accounts for bills and obligations that cannot wait.

The author defines debt as money owed. The [Chapter 1 map](/docs/chapters/start-where-you-are#what-counts-as-debt) includes borrowed money, unpaid bills, and taxes, fines, and court-ordered amounts. The author's target is income without debt; the repayment sequence still needs evidence and context.

## Story and exercise [#story-and-exercise]

The author's experience of living on credit after losing a job is source material for this section. Keep it tied to [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3).

The first exercise can ask the reader to list each debt, balance, rate, payment, and due date. The later steps for choosing a repayment order need evidence and worked examples.

# The life you want (/docs/topics/dream-lifestyle)



**Chapter destination:** [2. The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want). These are supporting notes for the manuscript.

Early source exercise based on [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3), retained for reference. The developed version is now in [Chapter 2](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want), with a worked example, research notes, and [workbook pages 5–7](/docs/workbook#chapter-2-the-life-you-want). Use those pages for the current exercise.

## Start with a day [#start-with-a-day]

Think about the life you want. Get specific.

What time do you wake up? Where do you live? What work do you do? Think about your family, your home, your travel, and the things you choose to spend money on.

You might want to get up at 5:30, go to the gym, and take your kids to school. You might want to do your job and get home in time for dinner. That is one of the lives described in the recording. Yours can look different.

Write out your own day before you put a number on it.

## Put a cost on it [#put-a-cost-on-it]

Use your own estimates in one currency. Worked examples will use generic $ amounts. Note which costs you have checked and which are still guesses.

| Part of your life                   | What you want | Estimated monthly cost | Where the estimate comes from |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Home                                |               |                        |                               |
| Food and household costs            |               |                        |                               |
| Getting around                      |               |                        |                               |
| Family and care                     |               |                        |                               |
| Health                              |               |                        |                               |
| Travel and time off                 |               |                        |                               |
| Clothes, hobbies, and other choices |               |                        |                               |
| Other costs from your own list      |               |                        |                               |

For a cost that happens once a year, record that annual amount and its monthly share. Keep one-time purchases on a separate list so you can see what is recurring.

## Compare it with where you are [#compare-it-with-where-you-are]

Write down your current income and debt beside your estimate. Identify your [reader path](/docs/reader-paths).

The gap gives the rest of the workbook a job. It helps you see which questions to work on: earning income, changing expenses, handling debt, or revisiting the life you described.

This early worksheet is not a complete income target. The developed Chapter 2 exercise accounts for saving, payments, costs or tax still to cover, and one-time goals without counting them twice. Unknowns keep the comparison provisional.

## Why this sits near the start [#why-this-sits-near-the-start]

In Note 3, the author first talks about maximizing income and reducing debt. He then corrects himself: the larger goal is to define the life you want and calculate what it takes.

The book plan follows that correction. The exercise gives the reader a direction; their current situation determines the next step.

# Growing your income (/docs/topics/income)



**Chapter destination:** [3. Find and grow your income](/docs/chapters/grow-your-income). The chapter now has a first draft, a [spoken adaptation](/docs/scripts/grow-your-income), and workbook pages [8](/docs/workbook/my-income-options) and [9](/docs/workbook/my-next-income-step). These remain supporting source notes.

## The point from Note 3 [#the-point-from-note-3]

The written plan says increasing monthly income is the number-one priority. In the recording, that priority depends on where the reader starts.

For someone with no income, the author puts getting income first. For someone who already has income, he connects earning more to the life they want and the skills they are willing to learn.

The author then corrects the larger goal: work out the life you want and what it costs. That gives the income discussion a purpose.

## What to cover [#what-to-cover]

* Finding income when the reader has none.
* Ways to grow income from hourly work, a salary, or a business.
* The skills, time, and tradeoffs involved in each option.
* Why a business or a full-time job will not suit everyone.
* How this connects to the reader's own lifestyle calculation.

The first chapter draft develops these steps, including a fictional editing test and the limits around work, costs, support, and payment timing. [Research notes](/docs/research#chapter-3-choosing-an-income-step) record the primary-source checks. Actual pay, hiring, business results, and support eligibility remain specific to the reader.

## Story to develop [#story-to-develop]

[Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) describes losing a job during a honeymoon, moving to New York, and facing higher bills while carrying debt. It can ground the no-income path. Confirm the timeline and figures before using the full story.

Sources: [Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) and [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan).


# Topic notes (/docs/topics)



These are working notes behind the [12 chapters](/docs/chapters). Each page links to its chapter destination. The [book plan](/docs/outline) places smaller questions inside those chapters.

Most pages are writing briefs. The life-you-want page includes a draft exercise drawn from Note 3. Factual chapters need sources and worked examples before they are ready for readers.

# Investing 101 (/docs/topics/investing)



**Chapter destination:** [11. Before you invest](/docs/chapters/before-you-invest) and [12. Ways to invest](/docs/chapters/ways-to-invest). These are supporting notes for the manuscript.

## What to cover [#what-to-cover]

The written plan includes stocks, real estate, crypto, and investing in businesses. Each needs a plain explanation, an example, and an account of how money can be gained or lost.

[Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) also asks about index funds, bonds, Treasuries, private equity, and hedge funds. Chapter 12 includes these within its sections, with private equity and hedge funds as reference material.

## Connect it to the reader's situation [#connect-it-to-the-readers-situation]

The timing of this topic depends on the reader's income, debt, goals, and circumstances. Build and research those connections before writing a rule about when everyone should invest.

## Source material and gaps [#source-material-and-gaps]

[Note 1](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-1) mentions the author's investing experience and his mother's real estate experience. Those are leads for stories, not evidence for an investment claim.

The chapter still needs sources, risk explanations, country-specific details, and worked examples.

Source plan: [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan).


# Your mindset about money (/docs/topics/money-mindset)



**Chapter destination:** [2. The life you want](/docs/chapters/the-life-you-want). These are supporting notes for the manuscript.

## The point from the recordings [#the-point-from-the-recordings]

People want different things from money. In [Note 1](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-1), the author names security, travel, cars, watches, and medical bills for family. He does not want people shamed for choosing a different goal.

[Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2) makes room for changes over time. Someone's current situation does not describe the rest of their life.

## Draft passage [#draft-passage]

You might want to travel. You might want to know your bills are covered. You might want to be home for dinner with your family.

Start there. What do you want your money to help you do?

The answer does not have to match anyone else's.

## Develop next [#develop-next]

Connect this stance to the [life you want exercise](/docs/topics/dream-lifestyle). The broader claim that mindset affects money decisions needs examples and evidence. Keep the reader's circumstances in view; avoid implying that a change in attitude alone resolves a money problem.

Source plan: [General plan](/docs/raw-thoughts/general-plan).


# Companion workbook (/docs/workbook)



The book walks you through each step. This workbook gives you a place to put your answers.

When a chapter sends you to a workbook page, fill it out here. Keep your pages so you can come back to them when your life changes.

**Don't have the companion workbook?** A notebook or plain paper works too. The book tells you what to write. You can do every exercise without the workbook. You can also use a document if writing by hand doesn't work for you.

Write what you know. Leave details blank or write “not sure yet” when you need to come back to them. An unknown amount isn't zero.

# 11. My bill calendar (/docs/workbook/my-bill-calendar)



**Workbook page 11 · Chapter 4, Steps 3 and 5**

Use [Chapter 4's timing example](/docs/chapters/when-you-get-paid#a-month-can-work-while-a-week-doesnt) and [page 10](/docs/workbook/my-next-payment-plan). Plain paper works with the same columns.

Period: \_\_\_\_\_ · Currency: \_\_\_\_\_ · Cash/accounts covered: \_\_\_\_\_

Opening available cash, matching page 10: $\_\_\_\_\_

Amounts reserved outside this calendar: \_\_\_\_\_

## Dates and balances [#dates-and-balances]

Add rows as needed. Enter separate rows for each receipt, bill, and other planned use. Write the date funds must be available, allowing time for the payment to reach its destination. Record the bill's due date as well.

| Money in or use | Due date, if any | Date received / to send or set aside | In | Out or reserved | Running amount left for this plan | Expected / confirmed / paid, and automatic? |
| --------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ | -- | --------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Opening cash    |                  |                                      |    |                 | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |
|                 |                  |                                      | $  | $               | $                                 |                                             |

Running amount = previous amount + money in − money out or newly reserved. A forecast receipt stays marked expected until it arrives. If it is late, recalculate.

A reservation is counted once: don't subtract it again when paying from that reserved money. This calendar tracks money left for this plan, which can differ from the balance shown by your bank. Transfers between included accounts don't change their combined balance. Keep them labeled rather than counting them as new income or duplicate spending.

First date with a gap, and its amount: \_\_\_\_\_

Later bill or next-period cost that needs money held now: \_\_\_\_\_

Date change requested / provider / response / new terms and effective date: \_\_\_\_\_

Keep the existing date until a change is confirmed.

## Payday review [#payday-review]

Amount actually received and date: \_\_\_\_\_

Differences from the plan and changes made: \_\_\_\_\_

Payments and transfers completed and checked: \_\_\_\_\_

Money still reserved and what it must cover: \_\_\_\_\_

Next review date: \_\_\_\_\_

Use [page 12](/docs/workbook/when-money-falls-short) for any uncovered need or negative running amount.

# 8. My income options (/docs/workbook/my-income-options)



**Workbook page 8 · Chapter 3, Steps 1–3**

## What has to fit [#what-has-to-fit]

| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- |

| Is that amount gross, after costs, or after costs and tax?                |          |          |
| Costs or tax still to cover; known or unknown?                            |          |          |
| Amount left after known costs and tax; provisional if anything is unknown |          |          |
| Earliest payment date and how certain it is                               |          |          |
| Fit with my schedule and responsibilities                                 |          |          |
| One small action to check this option                                     |          |          |

If only one option is feasible, why? \_\_\_\_\_

Keep these possible earnings separate from current income. Compare the same time periods and count each cost once. Use [page 9](/docs/workbook/my-next-income-step) to choose an action.

# Adding new thoughts (/docs/writing-plan)



## Incorporation plan · October 1, 2026 [#incorporation-plan--october-1-2026]

Six recordings are saved in full as [Notes 4–9](/docs/raw-thoughts). This batch adds raw source scripts and a plan for developing them. Chapters 2–8 now have first drafts, spoken adaptations, and workbook exercises. The recording-based drafting sequence below is complete as a first pass. Each note keeps the spoken restarts and corrections, with time markers and a separate list of uncertain wording.

The script outlines below are proposed speaking beats for the same chapter material. They are not quotations or finished scripts. Keep the existing 12 chapters and the book's aim: define the life you want, work out what it takes, and choose the next step from where you are.

### Voice revision · October 1, 2026 [#voice-revision--october-1-2026]

The author asked for fuller, more natural explanations while keeping the compact book pace. The [writing guide](/docs/writing-style) now uses clear adult language and connected reasoning, without a school-grade target, sentence-length limit, or comma limit.

The two opening pages and Chapters 1–8 have received a voice revision against Notes 1–9. The pass restores source-backed reactions, concrete situations, meaningful repetition, and admissions; moves transcript and production commentary to end notes; and preserves the worked examples, reader paths, financial qualifications, and workbook references. Chapters 9–12 remain planned rather than drafted.

Validation for this revision: the local production build passed, and all 524 checked internal links and anchors resolved. The bundled preservation check passed for all ten revised chapter/front-matter pages, including unchanged headings, tables, frontmatter, and original link targets. Number-count warnings were reviewed: they concern removed repetition and source-label wording, not changed calculations. Two chapter-editing workstreams were integrated and reviewed against the source notes; a separate read-only review checked the opening and Chapters 4 and 8. No CI run or publication was triggered.

A follow-up pass now covers the remaining technical explanations, worked-example commentary, transitions, and exercise instructions throughout Chapters 1–8. Exercises were rewritten as guided steps while preserving their required fields, decisions, exceptions, workbook references, and plain-paper alternatives. Strong passages from the first voice revision were retained. Tables and calculations remain unchanged. The follow-up passed the local production build, structural preservation checks for all eight chapters, and the internal-link check. The existing spoken scripts still reflect the earlier prose pass. Their examples and exercise references remain applicable, but their wording has not received this revision. The print PDFs are earlier layout proofs and do not include the revised Chapter 1 prose. Author review and later script/print synchronization remain.

1. **Chapter 2 — Know what you want.** Start with “What was your plan?” Connect the current money picture to a detailed future day. Develop one settled version of Michelle as an explicitly fictional example. Price the whole household plan, state what a partner covers, and separate monthly costs from one-time purchases. End with the gap between today's situation and the target. Exercise: desired day, costs, assumptions, and target date.
2. **Chapter 3 — Get income now; choose a route for later.** Keep Notes 5–6's urgency and Note 5's care for students and stay-at-home parents. Fit the steps to the existing no-income paths and support sources; account for ability, care duties, work costs, and access. Then use the vehicle analogy and the author's founder-versus-product-work reflection. Compare possible routes without promising that writing, posting, or building an app guarantees earnings. End with one action, its cost, and a review date. Exercise: current options, required skills, constraints, and a next step.
3. **Chapter 4 — Make a plan before the money arrives.** Follow Note 9's own correction at 03:12–03:26: list mandatory bills before choosing a saving amount. Build a payment calendar, then show an affordable saving choice and room for chosen spending. Keep the tithing passage in the author's first-person faith perspective, with its own example. Add a separate shortfall case so the saving percentages never become an instruction to miss essential payments. Exercise: take-home income, commitments, due dates, chosen saving/giving, and the remainder.
4. **Chapters 5–7 — Understand the bill and the borrowing.** Explain the terms before using the author's rewards and spending examples. Chapter 5 owns borrowing comparisons, including overdrafts and lines of credit. Chapter 6 owns card costs, statements, minimum payments, and the payment decision. Chapter 7 owns scores and reports. Proposed script sequence: what you borrowed → what it costs → what is due → what gets reported. Exercise: a card/borrowing record with balance labels, rate, fees, minimum due, and dates.
5. **Chapter 8 — Decide before you buy.** Present “afford it twice” as the author's personal rule for unplanned purchases, using his corrected $250 threshold. Keep the distinction between saved-for purchases and impulse buys. Use the $350 headphones / $700 example, then the expected freelance-payment story, BNPL obligations, and the car discussion. Label illustrative details in the freelance story rather than claiming every number and purchase was a documented event. End with a purchase decision sheet that includes existing commitments and the full cost.

For every chapter, write the prose first, then adapt the same sourced material into a spoken script with an opening question, one example, a practical step, and an exercise. Keep the author's candor and faith. Remove filler in developed prose while retaining the full source notes. Link each developed passage to its note and relevant time range.

Add companion-workbook pages only when these exercises are drafted. Choose the next unused page numbers then, and give the same instructions for plain paper. Pages 1–4 stay attached to Chapter 1. Pages 5–7 accompany Chapter 2; pages 8–9 accompany Chapter 3; pages 10–18 accompany Chapters 4–8.

### Example and claim checks [#example-and-claim-checks]

* **Michelle and the income examples:** settle her fictional background; recheck the cleaning amount ($20 or $200 a week); resolve the $6,500/$600 target change; rebuild the tax, sales, and app-subscription examples. Keep gross revenue, business costs, taxes, and personal income separate. Do not carry over guaranteed audience or earnings claims.
* **Payday examples:** the first settled illustration is $5,000 take-home minus $2,500 bills minus $1,250 saving, leaving $1,250. The smaller-surplus example changes from $500 to $300 to $400 in speech; choose and label one set of assumptions. Specify whether a percentage applies to take-home income, income after giving, or the remainder after bills. For the tithing example, $5,000 minus $500 leaves $4,500 before bills and saving; rebuild the rest explicitly rather than reusing the original remainder.
* **Card and score explanations:** recheck the garbled spending rule and the soft-check/report passages. Research minimum payments versus paying the statement balance, interest and grace periods, product terms, score models, reporting, and country-specific rules. The author's Amex offer and remembered book passage are source leads, not verified current advice.
* **Purchases and shortfalls:** define the limits of the author's personal rules. Research full ownership costs, BNPL terms, payment-date changes, and consequences of missed payments before providing step-by-step guidance.

The detailed evidence queue is in [Research notes](/docs/research#recording-research-queue). Unclear wording remains flagged in each raw note; a second automated pass did not settle every passage.

* Every new passage has a source note; uncertain speech is checked before it becomes a quote.

* Financial claims have current primary sources and a stated country or product scope where needed.
* Chapters, spoken scripts, workbook references, and plain-paper exercises agree.
* The author can review prose separately from the preserved raw recordings.

## Bring the next recording here [#bring-the-next-recording-here]

Attach an audio file in the Codex chat for this project. You can talk through one topic or several. Add context if you want a specific focus.

The assistant will transcribe the recording, save it as the next numbered note, and use the [book plan](/docs/outline) to place its ideas. You do not have to name a destination for every thought.

## What happens to a recording [#what-happens-to-a-recording]

1. Save the full transcript in [Raw thoughts](/docs/raw-thoughts) as the next numbered note. Notes 1–9 are now saved; the next is Note 10.
2. Read it for ideas, examples, stories, and claims.
3. Update the relevant topic or draft chapter in the author's voice. Add or revise its companion-workbook page when an exercise needs answer space. Keep plain-paper instructions in the book.
4. Link the new prose back to the source note.
5. Put factual questions in [Research notes](/docs/research).
6. Report which book pages changed and what still needs clarification.

If one recording covers several topics, its ideas can go in several pages. The full transcript stays together as the source.

## Keep the voice [#keep-the-voice]

Follow the [writing guide](/docs/writing-style) and compare new prose with Notes 1–9. The October 1 voice update applies to both chapters and spoken scripts: keep the author's questions, everyday examples, directness, admissions, and meaningful qualifications. Clean up speech while preserving its natural rhythm. Give existing drafts the same voice pass as they are revised.

When an unclear word or a conflict could change the meaning, flag it for review. Do not silently decide what the author meant.

# Writing guide (/docs/writing-style)



## The voice [#the-voice]

Write like the author is talking to one person. Use “you” when speaking to the reader and “I” for the author's own experience. Contractions fit. Plain words fit. The tone is direct and candid, with room for warmth and a short aside.

Use [Notes 1–9](/docs/raw-thoughts) as the voice reference. The author's October 1, 2026 revision direction is to make the book easy to understand and follow while sounding more like his speech. There is no school-grade reading target. Preserve his way of explaining, questioning, and reacting when cleaning up the words. The reader should hear someone working through a decision with them.

[Note 1](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-1) gives the stance: “I'm also still trying to figure it out as well.” Keep that openness. Do not turn the author into someone who has solved every money problem.

[Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2) says, “We have ups and we have downs.” The author talks about money as something that changes over a person's life. He gives the reader room to start again.

[Note 3](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-3) moves from an idea to a specific life: getting up, going to the gym, taking the kids to school, working, and eating with family. Keep that habit of making an idea concrete.

## What sounds like the author [#what-sounds-like-the-author]

* **Start with the question someone would ask.** Note 4 asks what the plan was. Note 9 asks what happens when there isn't enough to pay the bills. Use a question to open the actual problem, then spend time answering it. Avoid adding a question to every paragraph.
* **Walk through it together.** “Okay, so,” “let's say,” “right?” and “now” are natural parts of the recordings. Keep a few where they move the explanation along or invite the reader to check the reasoning. Do not sprinkle them into every sentence.
* **Make the situation visible.** Note 4 gives Michelle a workday, children to pick up, and things she wants to afford. Note 9 uses bills, headphones, a camera, and a payment that hasn't arrived. Show the choice in someone's day before naming an abstract principle.
* **Say what you think.** Keep “for me,” “I think,” and “what I would do” when they distinguish personal judgment from a fact. Note 9 explicitly calls the tithing passage a personal belief. Do not edit those qualifications into universal instructions.
* **Keep the push and the admission.** Notes 6 and 9 can be blunt. Note 9 also admits that the author doesn't get his own purchase rule right every time. Preserve both sides of that voice. A warning should explain the decision and its consequence; do not invent insults or make every section a telling-off.
* **Give people room.** Note 5 respects stay-at-home parents. Note 9 acknowledges that sometimes the proposed saving amount isn't possible. Keep those conditions beside the advice they qualify, with the same weight as the forceful line.

These are patterns to listen for, not a template every section must follow. Notes 4–9 are automated transcripts with flagged uncertainties. Use clear passages for voice; do not copy a transcription error as a personal mannerism.

## Make it easy to read [#make-it-easy-to-read]

Write for an adult who may be new to money topics. Assume intelligence without assuming financial knowledge. Use familiar language, explain unfamiliar terms, and give the reader enough reasoning to follow the decision. A grade score, sentence length, or comma count does not decide whether a passage is clear.

* Use active voice and simple tenses.
* Prefer present tense for guidance. Use past tense when a real story needs it.
* Vary sentence length with the thought. Keep a cause, its consequence, and a useful qualification together when that makes the explanation easier to follow. Use a short sentence when it deserves emphasis. Do not break ordinary lists or connected ideas into fragments.
* Choose everyday words. Explain financial terms when the reader first meets them.
* Cut empty intensifiers and repeated filler. Keep a word such as “honestly” or “actually” when it carries the author's reaction or a meaningful correction.
* Give each paragraph one main idea and enough development to make it useful. Connect it to the paragraph before it; avoid a sequence of detached tips.
* Explain why a step matters before asking the reader to do it. Keep numbered steps for exercises and sequences, and tables for comparisons and calculations.
* Carry the same voice through technical sections and exercises. Preserve the required action and its conditions, but explain how to do it in connected prose. Accuracy protects the meaning; it does not require keeping a stiff sentence or a cluster of commands unchanged.

Keep the rhythm natural. A paragraph can follow the author through a situation, his reaction, and the reason for his advice. It does not have to end with a slogan or a question. Leave room for a short aside or meaningful repetition when the source earns it.

Keep the book's compact pace. Expand a passage when the reasoning is missing, and cut repeated instructions or summaries that add nothing. Do not pad chapters to reach a page count, and do not compress a useful explanation just to keep it short.

## Keep the reasoning and personality together [#keep-the-reasoning-and-personality-together]

The recordings often move from a concrete situation to the author's reaction, then to advice and a qualification or admission. Preserve that movement where it exists. His admission that he has spent money before a freelance payment arrived gives weight to his warning about doing it. Extracting only the warning loses part of the explanation.

Keep specific details that do useful work: school pickup, the car someone wants, a sale that tempts him to break his own rule. Keep his humor and firm opinions when supported by the notes. Do not soften every reaction into neutral advice, and do not manufacture a stronger opinion than he expressed. “Bro,” questions, and profanity cannot substitute for his way of thinking through the problem.

When the source only asks a question and leaves the answer for research, explain the verified answer through that practical question. Do not invent a personal experience to make a researched section feel conversational. Necessary conditions, risks, and country-specific limits remain beside the claims they qualify.

## What to preserve from the recordings [#what-to-preserve-from-the-recordings]

Keep the author's point of view, faith, personal experience, and respect for different goals. Keep a blunt phrase or a casual word when it carries his voice. Use profanity only when it comes from the source and belongs in the passage; do not add it to manufacture personality.

Words such as “stuff,” “things,” “bro,” and “that's okay” can stay when they fit the passage. Do not replace every everyday word with formal language. Use a precise financial term where the distinction matters, and explain it. Slang and profanity are occasional choices, not a quota or a substitute for an explanation.

Keep God, church, and the author's Christian perspective where he brings them into the material. Preserve his stated belief and its scope. Keep his admissions about debt and mistakes too. Do not give him a polished success story or authority that he hasn't claimed.

Use stories and numbers the author supplied. Label invented worked examples as examples and use generic $ amounts, as requested in [Plan decisions](/docs/raw-thoughts/plan-decisions). Keep real source figures intact with their original context. Use one currency within a calculation; generic dollars do not make legal or tax rules universal.

## How to turn speech into prose [#how-to-turn-speech-into-prose]

Keep the full transcript in Raw thoughts. In the book draft, remove false starts and repeated filler. Add punctuation and paragraph breaks. Keep repetition when it adds emphasis or explains an idea.

Keep a repeated phrase when the second use earns its place. Note 9's “they stack up” makes accumulated payments feel concrete; several repeats of “super” can usually become one. Remove recording logistics such as “as this is being transcribed” from reader-facing prose. Use a settled correction in the draft, while keeping its original wording and correction together in the raw note.

Keep production commentary out of the chapter's explanation. Put transcript timestamps, uncertain source wording, reconstruction history, and reminders to the editor in the end source notes. Keep source links there so passages remain traceable. A brief label such as “a fictional example in generic dollars” belongs beside a worked example; a sentence about what was or was not checked in the recording does not. Factual citations can stay beside the claims they support without interrupting the author to describe the research process.

Do not guess at unclear transcription. Mark it for review. Do not invent a personal story, a result, a belief, or a fact to make a paragraph stronger.

The author's claims still need evidence. If a new recording disagrees with a drafted section, record the conflict and resolve it from the source or ask one focused question.

Confidence of delivery does not settle a claim. Keep personal rules labeled as personal rules. Check numbers and financial explanations through the [research record](/docs/research). Source an anecdote before writing it in the first person; never add an experience just to make the prose sound more personal.

## A voice example [#a-voice-example]

Edited from [Note 2](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-2):

> We have ups and we have downs. You can earn a good income and still struggle to get to the next payday, so I want you to have something you can use wherever you are right now. Work through the part that fits your situation, put it into practice, and come back when you need the next part. You're probably not going to remember every single thing in here anyway.

This is a draft example of the author's voice, not a quote from the recording.

## More examples from the recordings [#more-examples-from-the-recordings]

These are short edited voice samples, not verbatim quotations or finished chapter passages. They keep the source's meaning while removing restarts.

From [Note 4](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-4), around 03:08–03:47:

> Okay, so let's work backwards. Where would you love to be five or ten years from now? What does that life look like? Then we can figure out what you need to do to get there.

From [Note 9](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-9), around 14:01–14:36:

> Sometimes you don't have enough money to pay all your bills. What happens then? I'm not going to sit here and pretend that never happens. When I'm in that situation, I look at what I absolutely need to pay.

From [Note 9](/docs/raw-thoughts/note-9), around 25:04–end:

> I love cars, and I'm not going to pretend I don't care which one I drive. They make me happy. You might care about something completely different, and that's fine, because your quality of life matters too. But if getting the car means you can't enjoy driving it because you're worried about the payments, we need to look at that before you buy it.

The first sample thinks through a goal with the reader. The second keeps the author's experience beside the difficult situation. The third lets him have a preference without turning it into a rule for everyone.

## Book prose and spoken scripts [#book-prose-and-spoken-scripts]

Use the same voice in both. In the book, trim enough repetition that the reader can follow the thought on the first pass. In a spoken script, leave room for a pause, an aside, or a repeated line that helps someone listening. Do not turn the book into formal finance copy or the scripts into an exaggerated version of the author.

Before finishing a passage, read it aloud and check:

1. Does this sound like something the author could say in Notes 1–9?
2. Did the edit keep his opinion, faith, admissions, and meaningful conditions?
3. Is the example concrete, with its source and any uncertainty accounted for?
4. Did the edit remove filler without removing all the conversational rhythm?
5. Is each personal claim supported by his source material, and each factual claim checked?
6. Can a reader new to this subject follow why one thought leads to the next?
7. Have production notes stayed out of the explanation, with necessary factual conditions still visible?

Apply this guide when drafting and revising the chapters and scripts in the [writing plan](/docs/writing-plan). Track completed revisions there; a guide change alone does not establish that a chapter or script has been revised.

Those references record the earlier approach. The author's later direction replaces the grade target and sentence/comma rules. Use his recordings and the clarity checks above to govern the prose; do not imitate the public figure in the references.
